preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Caroline is now in her last year of the Nursing program. She tells you that with her night shifts in the hospital, she has been forgetting to take her contraceptive pills (Yasmin). She had unprotected intercourse 3 days ago and can’t remember when was the last day she took her pill. She asks you about emergency contraceptive options and other options for contraceptive methods. Her medical history is unremarkable. However, she gained significant weight in the past few years.

stem: Which longer-term contraceptive options would be suitable for Caroline? What factors guided your choices?

options.html: A repeat Yasmin prescription with a phone alarm set around her night shifts
The progestin only mini-pill, being more forgiving of a late or missed dose
The combined transdermal patch, which removes daily dosing altogether
A long acting method, since daily dosing is what failed and weight matters

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Two features of her story drive the choice, and the deck puts both on the case summary slide: ⭐ night shifts with compliance problems, and ⭐ significant weight gain.

>

> Compliance rules out anything daily. That points at the long-acting methods - the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, the etonogestrel implant, or the DMPA injection every three months.

>

> ⚠ B is the trap, and it inverts the truth. The mini-pill is the least forgiving method there is: ⭐ missed by more than 3 hours means backup contraception is needed. For someone working night shifts it is the worst available choice.

>

> C fails on her second feature - ⭐ the patch may be less effective above 90 kg, and it also carries more VTE risk than the pill because it bypasses first-pass metabolism, not less. A repeats what has already failed.

>

> ⚠ One caution worth voicing: the injection and the implant both list weight gain among their effects, and she has raised weight unprompted - so of the long-acting methods the intrauterine system is the one to lead with.

>

> Principle: when adherence is the failure, remove the daily decision - then pick between the long-acting methods on the side effect she cares about.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Patricia is 49-year-old women who presents to your office for counselling on contraceptive methods. She is in a new relationship after a divorce and is sexually active. She reports that her menstrual periods are less regular than previously, she’s been experiencing trouble sleeping for the past 6 months and more acne on her chin. She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: Does Patricia present a contraindication for combined or progestin-only contraceptive?

options.html: No absolute contraindication - her pressure is controlled, she is a non-smoker
Yes, her hypertension is an absolute contraindication to both types of method here
Yes, her age by itself rules out every hormonal method available to her now
No, and her hypertension has no bearing on the choice between the two types

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ Contraindications are graded on the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC), and the grade is the answer rather than a yes or no:

>

> ① no restriction · ② advantages generally outweigh the risks · ③ risks usually outweigh the advantages · ④ unacceptable health risk, the true absolute contraindication.

>

> ⭐ Hypertension crosses from relative to absolute at ≥ 160 systolic or ≥ 100 diastolic. Patricia is 130/80 on enalapril, so she is nowhere near that line. She is a non-smoker with a BMI of 24, and she has no migraine with aura and no thromboembolic history - ⭐ the two category ④ entries that matter most, and both apply to combined methods only.

>

> ⚠ D overshoots in the other direction. Her hypertension is not an absolute contraindication, but it is not irrelevant either: it is a genuine consideration on the combined side, and it is one reason a progestin-only method is easy to justify. ⭐ Almost every entry in the combined column is there because of the estrogen, which is why the answer to *"what can she have instead?"* is nearly always progestin-only or intrauterine.

>

> Principle: read hypertension against the 160/100 threshold, and remember the combined column is an estrogen column.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Patricia is 49-year-old women who presents to your office for counselling on contraceptive methods. She is in a new relationship after a divorce and is sexually active. She reports that her menstrual periods are less regular than previously, she’s been experiencing trouble sleeping for the past 6 months and more acne on her chin. She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: What are the advantages and disadvantages of combined versus progestin-only contraceptives in Patricia's situation?

options.html: Progestin-only controls her cycle and acne better, but raises her clot risk
Combined treats her cycle, acne and symptoms but adds estrogen risk at 49
Neither has an advantage here, so the decision rests on her preference alone
Combined is contraindicated by her age, so only progestin-only can be offered

answer:
The correct answer is B.

Her three complaints are the advantages column, and her age is the disadvantages column.

>

> What combined offers her. Cycle control for periods that are less regular than they were · ⭐ drospirenone is the anti-androgenic progestin, the one to reach for in hormonal acne - and she has new acne on her chin · and the estrogen helps the perimenopausal symptoms behind her disturbed sleep. The general benefits also apply: ⭐ reduced ovarian and endometrial cancer, reduced dysmenorrhea, lighter and more predictable periods.

>

> What combined costs her. ⭐ Increased VTE risk, and at 49 the background risk is no longer trivial. Her hypertension sits alongside it.

>

> Progestin-only inverts both: ⭐ no increased VTE risk - except the injection, and except drospirenone or cyproterone preparations - but it does little for cycle control and nothing for her acne.

>

> ⚠ A states the trade backwards, which is the point of including it: it is progestin-only that avoids the clot risk, and combined that controls the cycle.

>

> Principle: weigh her symptoms, which want estrogen, against her age and pressure, which do not - and weigh both against the risks of pregnancy, not against zero.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Patricia is 49-year-old women who presents to your office for counselling on contraceptive methods. She is in a new relationship after a divorce and is sexually active. She reports that her menstrual periods are less regular than previously, she’s been experiencing trouble sleeping for the past 6 months and more acne on her chin. She asks about the risks of using hormonal contraceptives at her age. Patricia is non-smoker. She was diagnosed with hypertension 4 years ago, but it is healthy otherwise. Physical Examination: BMI 24, BP 130/80. Medication Hx: Enalapril (for hypertension), Ibuprofen (as needed for back pain and menstrual cramps)

stem: Does the choice of delivery system (pill, injection, intrauterine device) make a difference for Patricia, and why?

options.html: No, because all three deliver equivalent systemic doses of the same hormones
Yes, because only the injection escapes first pass hepatic metabolism entirely
Yes - route changes the estrogen exposure, the adherence needed and the effect
No, provided she is willing to take a tablet at the same time every single day

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Route is not a packaging decision, and three separate things move with it.

>

> - Estrogen exposure. ⭐ The patch and the ring bypass first-pass metabolism, and that - not the dose - is why they carry more VTE risk than the pill. ⚠ B has this exactly backwards: bypassing first pass raises the risk, and the injection is a progestin anyway

> - Adherence. A daily pill, a three-monthly injection and a multi-year device make completely different demands

> - What else it treats. ⭐ The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is listed for heavy bleeding as well as contraception, and is ⭐ more effective than the pill at blocking folliculogenesis because it delivers a high progestin dose at the uterus

>

> ⚠ One caution against the injection at her age: ⭐ DMPA is the exception among progestin-only methods for VTE risk, and the injection and implant may contribute to bone loss - which matters more at 49, approaching menopause, than it would at 25.

>

> Principle: the route decides the estrogen risk, the adherence burden and whether her bleeding gets treated at the same time.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 37-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. She reports nocturia and urinary frequency. Her physician ordered a colonoscopy, ultrasonography and prescribed her a medication to reduce the heavy bleeding while they wait for the results. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and is not planning to become pregnant.

stem: Describe the pharmacological basis underlying the use of tranexamic acid and naproxen to reduce heavy bleeding.

options.html: Both inhibit cyclooxygenase, so both reduce prostaglandin driven uterine cramping
Tranexamic acid inhibits cyclooxygenase; naproxen stabilises the clot that forms
Both act on the endometrium directly, thinning it so that there is less to shed
Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding; naproxen inhibits cyclooxygenase

answer:
The correct answer is D.

Two unrelated mechanisms that happen to converge on the same symptom.

>

> Tranexamic acid is an ⭐ antifibrinolytic: it blocks the plasminogen lysine-binding site, so plasminogen is not converted to plasmin, so ⭐ the clot that has formed is not broken down. It does nothing to the cause - ⭐ it is symptomatic only, which is exactly why it suits a patient who is waiting for results.

>

> Naproxen is a non-selective NSAID: it ⭐ reduces prostaglandin synthesis through non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition, which reduces uterine cramping and also reduces heavy bleeding. That it treats her cramps at the same time is a convenience rather than a coincidence.

>

> ⭐ Neither shrinks a fibroid, and neither treats a cause - and that is the setup for the next question in the case, where the ultrasound comes back.

>

> Principle: tranexamic acid protects the clot, naproxen removes the prostaglandins - both buy time, neither changes the diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 37-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anemia. She reports nocturia and urinary frequency. Her physician ordered a colonoscopy, ultrasonography and prescribed her a medication to reduce the heavy bleeding while they wait for the results. She takes a combined oral contraceptive and is not planning to become pregnant.

stem: Does this patient present any contraindications to these drugs?

options.html: Yes - her combined pill plus an antifibrinolytic compounds clot risk
Yes, her iron deficiency anemia is an absolute contraindication to both agents
No, neither drug carries any contraindication relevant to this patient at all
Yes, her urinary frequency indicates the renal impairment that rules out both

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The contraindication to tranexamic acid is a history of venous thromboembolism, and she has no such history - but she takes a combined oral contraceptive, and ⭐ combined hormonal contraception raises VTE risk by increasing factors VII, VIII, IX and X. Layering an antifibrinolytic on top of a prothrombotic pill is the interaction worth naming, and it is one the case sets up deliberately by telling you she is on a COC.

>

> For naproxen, the contraindications are ⭐ severe kidney disease, gastritis or peptic ulcer, and coagulopathies. None is stated for her.

>

> ⚠ D is the specific trap. Her nocturia and urinary frequency are pressure symptoms from the fibroids pressing on the bladder - the ultrasound confirms it two slides later. Reading them as renal impairment mistakes a mass effect for a creatinine. B inverts the logic: her anemia is the reason to treat, not a reason not to.

>

> Principle: read her medication list as part of the contraindication check, and read urinary symptoms in a fibroid case as pressure until proven otherwise.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A week later the results were available. The colonoscopy is negative. Ultrasonography shows a modestly enlarged uterus with three uterine fibroids.

stem: Which of the following drugs can be used to reduce the size of fibroids (select all that apply), and what is the pharmacological basis for their effect?

options.html: The intrauterine device, leuprolide and relugolix

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⚠ The source asks this as a select-all, which the house rule does not bank - so it is written here as a combinations question with the same content.

>

> ⭐ Only the GnRH-directed drugs shrink a fibroid. Everything else on the list treats the bleeding.

>

> | Drug | Effect on fibroid size | Why |

> | --- | --- | --- |

> | Tranexamic acid | none | antifibrinolytic, ⭐ symptomatic only |

> | Ibuprofen | none | reduces prostaglandins, so cramping and flow |

> | Levonorgestrel IUD | none | listed for heavy bleeding, not for size |

> | Leuprolide (agonist) | ⭐ yes | continuous dosing causes an initial flare, then receptor desensitisation and suppression |

> | Relugolix (antagonist) | ⭐ yes | ⭐ immediate receptor blockade - faster onset and NO flare, since no downregulation is needed |

>

> Both work the same way in the end: shut down gonadotropins, so the ovary stops making estrogen, so the estrogen-dependent fibroid shrinks. ⚠ The flare matters clinically - a GnRH agonist can transiently worsen a hormone-driven lesion before it helps, and an antagonist never does.

>

> Principle: fibroids are estrogen-dependent, so only the drugs that remove estrogen change their size.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: After her diagnosis, she was prescribed Relugolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate (a combination of a GnRH antagonist and low doses of steroid sex hormones).

stem: Why was estradiol and norethindrone added to her therapy?

options.html: To provide contraception, which the GnRH antagonist does not itself supply
To enhance the antagonist's effect on the fibroid by adding a second pathway
To offset the hypoestrogenic state, above all the bone loss it would cause
To prevent the initial gonadotropin flare that a GnRH antagonist would cause

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Relugolix works by producing a hypoestrogenic state, and that state is the treatment and the problem at once.

>

> ⭐ The hypoestrogenic profile is: bone loss, hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and mood and sleep change. Of those, ⭐ bone loss is the one that limits how long the drug can be given, because it is cumulative and silent.

>

> Giving back a low dose of estradiol with a progestin restores enough estrogen to protect the skeleton and settle the vasomotor symptoms, while leaving too little to re-grow the fibroid. The norethindrone is there for the usual reason a progestin accompanies estrogen: ⭐ unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia, so a woman with a uterus needs the progestin alongside it.

>

> ⚠ D describes the wrong drug class. ⭐ Antagonists never flare - that is an agonist problem, and it is one of the reasons to choose relugolix over leuprolide.

>

> ⚠ The vault note does not use the term "add-back" or carry this combination product by name, so the reasoning above is built from its hypoestrogenic adverse-effect profile rather than quoted. Worth confirming with the facilitator.

>

> Principle: you are deliberately inducing a menopause, so you give back just enough estrogen to protect the bone without feeding the fibroid.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: After her diagnosis, she was prescribed Relugolix/estradiol/norethindrone acetate (a combination of a GnRH antagonist and low doses of steroid sex hormones).

stem: Would she need to stop taking her combined oral contraceptives? Why?

options.html: No, the two are complementary and should deliberately be taken alongside it
No, but only if she reduces her combined pill to alternate days instead
Yes, since the combined pill would provoke a flare from the antagonist
Yes - the regimen already holds estrogen and a progestin, duplicating both

answer:
The correct answer is D.

The prescription is already three drugs in one tablet: a GnRH antagonist plus low doses of estradiol and norethindrone. Continuing a combined oral contraceptive on top means a second estrogen and a second progestin.

>

> Two problems follow:

>

> - The dose is the point. The added steroids are deliberately low - enough to protect bone, ⭐ too little to feed an estrogen-dependent fibroid. Adding a contraceptive dose of ethinyl estradiol on top defeats the reason the combination exists

> - Stacked estrogen is stacked risk, and ⭐ the VTE risk of combined hormonal contraception is its principal harm

>

> ⚠ D invents a mechanism. ⭐ Antagonists do not flare, and a combined pill would not cause one.

>

> ⚠ What this answer cannot settle is contraception. She is not planning to become pregnant, and the vault note does not state whether this combination is itself contraceptive - so stopping the pill leaves a question about what replaces it for that purpose, and a non-hormonal method is the obvious candidate. ⭐ Flagging that gap is part of the answer; filling it from outside the lecture is not.

>

> Principle: the add-back dose is calibrated, so anything stacked on top breaks the calibration - and stopping a contraceptive raises a contraceptive question.

stem: A 14-year-old girl comes in with a history of monthly cyclical abdominal pain. On examination, you note midline tenderness in the area below the umbilicus, and a purplish bulging at the vaginal introitus. Of the following, the most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

Every element is the outflow-tract column of the amenorrhea table.

>

> - ⭐ Cyclical pain with no bleeding is that column's named clue - the endometrium is cycling normally, blood is made but cannot get out

> - Purplish bulging at the introitus is retained blood behind an ⭐ imperforate hymen, the commonest outflow tract abnormality (1 in 2000)

> - Midline suprapubic tenderness is the distended vagina and uterus above it

>

> ⚠ The vault teaches this under hematometra and imperforate hymen rather than the word "hematocolpos" - colpos is the vagina, metra the uterus, and the same obstruction produces both.

>

> A has no uterus, so no cyclical pain and no trapped blood. B, C and E are not cyclical and not midline-obstructive; torsion in particular is acute and unilateral, not monthly.

>

> Principle: monthly pain with no period means the blood is being made and cannot leave - look at the introitus.

stem: A 15-year-old girl comes in for evaluation of infrequent menstrual periods. On examination, you note a BMI of 35 and acne. Otherwise, her examination is unremarkable. Of the following, what is the most likely laboratory abnormality associated with this patient's presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

Obesity + acne + infrequent rather than absent periods is the ⭐ eugonadotropic anovulation column, and that is where PCOS lives.

>

> The table's clues for it are exactly these: ⭐ hirsutism, acne, obesity, and cycles irregular rather than absent - and its next test is ⭐ testosterone, DHEA-S and 17-OHP. An elevated free testosterone is what that testing is looking for.

>

> A would mean the ovary has failed, which gives absent periods and vasomotor symptoms. D and E share a branch - ⭐ low T4 raises TRH, which raises both TSH and prolactin, and prolactin then suppresses GnRH - but neither explains obesity with acne. C is not a measurable clinical test.

>

> Principle: irregular rather than absent, with androgenic signs, is anovulation - and the androgen is what you measure.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is seen with a complaint of excessive bleeding with menses (menorrhagia). Of the following, which component of the history and examination most suggests von Willebrand disease?

options.html: Heavy flow from time of initial menses.

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ The discriminator is that it has been heavy since the very first period. An inherited bleeding disorder has been present her whole life, so there was never a normal baseline - whereas an acquired or structural cause has a before and an after.

>

> vWD sits in the ⭐ C - coagulopathy letter of PALM-COEIN, and it is the one to think of in an adolescent, because menarche is often the first haemostatic challenge she has ever faced.

>

> A points at immaturity of the axis, which is ⭐ the commonest cause of irregular bleeding in the first couple of years after menarche and is the competing answer here - but anovulatory bleeding is irregular, not uniformly heavy from the start. C suggests a structural or hormonal cause. D and E point elsewhere entirely.

>

> Principle: heavy from the first period ever is inherited until proven otherwise; heavy after a normal history is acquired.

stem: Of the following, which is the most appropriate first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandin-mediated, so the first-line treatment is the one that stops prostaglandin synthesis.

>

> The pharmacology lecture puts it directly: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis through non-selective cyclooxygenase inhibition, reducing uterine cramping, with dysmenorrhea named as the indication.

>

> ⚠ D is the strongest distractor and is not wrong in general - combined oral contraceptives are listed for dysmenorrhea too, and the lecture names it among their benefits. It is second line here: an NSAID is cheaper, immediate, taken only around the period, and needed for a trial before escalating. A has no anti-prostaglandin effect. C treats infection, which would make this secondary dysmenorrhea.

>

> Principle: primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandins, so block them first and reach for the pill when that fails.

preamble.html: Jessica is a 14 year old female coming to see you because she is concerned she has not started her period.

stem: Jessica is a 14 year old female coming to see you because she is concerned she has not started her period. What is the most first important thing to help guide intervention?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Breast development is the clinical readout of estrogen exposure, and estrogen status is what splits the differential before any blood test.

>

> - Thelarche present - the axis has worked, so at 14 she is inside the window (the threshold is 15 with secondary sex characteristics) and the question becomes outflow tract

> - Thelarche absent - the threshold is 13 without them, so she is already past it, and the problem is the ovary or above

>

> ⚠ A is the trap, and the distinction is worth holding. ⭐ Pubic hair is adrenal (adrenarche); breast development is ovarian (thelarche). Pubic hair can appear normally while the ovary does nothing - which is exactly the pattern in Erika's case later in this quiz, Tanner I breast with Tanner II pubic hair.

>

> C comes after the examination, not before it. D matters for short stature.

>

> Principle: stage the breast before you measure anything - it tells you whether estrogen has ever been present.

stem: Kaitlyn is a 16 year old female with a past medical history of type I diabetes. She comes to you today with concerns of irregular periods. She has not had her period for the past 3 months. Physical exam is unremarkable. The most important thing to rule out is:
answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ Rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. The vault states it twice over - "1st thing to rule out is PREGNANCY !!" and "beta hCG before anything else" - and it is the top branch of the whole flowchart.

>

> ⭐ Three months without menses after regular cycles is the definition of secondary amenorrhea, so this is not merely irregularity.

>

> ⚠ Her diabetes is there to pull you off it. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and travels with thyroid disease and primary ovarian insufficiency, so it invites a workup - but none of that changes what comes first. A, B and C are all reasonable entries on the differential and all of them are tested after the hCG.

>

> Principle: the test order is not the likelihood order - pregnancy is excluded first because missing it is the costliest error.

stem: Maggie is a 16 year old female who you are seeing for primary amenorrhea. Her physical exam and investigations are normal to date. A progesterone withdrawal test was performed and resulted in menstruation. The correct interpretation of this result is:

options.html: There is an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and patent outflow tract

answer:
The correct answer is C.

A withdrawal bleed is a functional test of three things at once, and passing it clears all three:

>

> - ⭐ There is estrogen - the progestin had a primed, proliferated endometrium to withdraw from. No estrogen means no lining, so nothing to shed

> - ⭐ The outflow tract is patent - the blood reached the outside

> - The axis is working well enough to have produced that estrogen

>

> What it shows is missing is ovulation, and therefore progesterone - which is the eugonadotropic anovulation column: ⭐ no ovulation → no progesterone → no withdrawal bleed, until you supply the progestin yourself.

>

> ⚠ B is the subtle one. She *is* short of progesterone, which is why the test works - but the option as written describes a systemic deficiency state, and the interpretation the test licenses is the positive one in C. A is what a negative test would suggest.

>

> Principle: a positive withdrawal bleed proves estrogen and a patent tract; what it reveals is anovulation.

stem: Lisa is 16 years old presenting with irregular periods. You have diagnosed her with PCOS. She is sexually active, and uses condoms regularly. You emphasize the importance of contraception despite the irregular menses. What is the best choice for contraception in this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The question asks for the best CONTRACEPTION, and that is not the same question as the best treatment for her PCOS. Read that way the answer follows: the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is a long-acting reversible method, the most effective class there is, and it removes the daily decision from a 16-year-old whose current method is condoms alone.

>

> It also does the second job PCOS demands. ⭐ Anovulation leaves estrogen unopposed, and unopposed estrogen is the road to endometrial hyperplasia - so whatever she uses has to protect the endometrium. The intrauterine system does that directly, delivering a high progestin dose at the uterus, and it is ⭐ more effective than the pill at blocking folliculogenesis for the same reason.

>

> ⚠ B is not a bad answer, and the source's own annotation says why it was tempting - beside the crossed-out pill it lists *regular menses, hyperandrogenism, endometrial protection*, which are exactly the three things a combined pill adds. ⭐ The pharmacology lecture names the COC as the treatment for PCOS (*COC or cyclic progestin - oppose the estrogen, protect the endometrium*), and In-Class - Amenorrhea says the same. So the lecture's PCOS answer and this quiz's contraception answer genuinely differ, and the stem's emphasis on contraception is what separates them.

>

> C causes weight gain and may contribute to bone loss, both poor in an adolescent. D is unreliable.

>

> Principle: asked for contraception in PCOS, reach for the LARC that also protects the endometrium; asked how to treat the PCOS, reach for the pill.

stem: Patricia is a 13 year old female who presents with a complaint of heavy periods. She started her period 3 months ago and finds that it last 7-9 days, and she has to change her pad every 2-3 hours. On exam, you notice petechiae on her lower legs. The most appropriate first test is:
answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The petechiae are the whole question. Heavy periods from menarche would already raise a coagulopathy; petechiae make it the leading diagnosis, and they point specifically at a platelet problem rather than a factor problem.

>

> A CBC answers two things in one cheap test:

>

> - The platelet count - thrombocytopenia, including ITP and leukemia, which the vault lists in the C - coagulopathy letter of PALM-COEIN

> - The haemoglobin - how much this bleeding has actually cost her, which decides urgency

>

> ⚠ Her bleeding is objectively heavy, not just described that way: ⭐ soaking a pad every 2-3 hours, for 7-9 days. The vault's AUB examination list names bruising and petechiae as the finding that signals coagulopathy.

>

> B and C investigate an axis that is producing periods perfectly well. D looks for structure in a 13-year-old three months post-menarche, where structural lesions are rare.

>

> Principle: petechiae plus heavy menses from menarche is a platelet count before anything else.

stem: Jackie is a 16 year old female who is presenting with complaints of irregular periods. What is the most important thing to establish?

options.html: Levels of FSH, LH, TSH and prolactin

answer:
The correct answer is C.

⭐ Time since menarche is what decides whether this is a disease at all. Cycles in the first couple of years after the first period are commonly anovulatory, because the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is still maturing - irregularity then is physiological.

>

> So the same complaint means two different things:

>

> | Menarche | Irregular cycles mean |

> | --- | --- |

> | Recent, within about 2 years | ⭐ normal immaturity of the axis - reassure and follow |

> | Years ago, cycles once regular | a change that needs a cause |

>

> ⚠ A is the right answer to a different question. Secondary sexual traits matter when periods have never started, as in Jessica's case at the top of this quiz. Jackie is menstruating, so development has plainly occurred. D is where the workup goes after this question is answered, and ordering it first risks investigating normal puberty. B matters for short stature.

>

> Principle: ask when the first period was - it separates an immature axis from a real disorder.

stem: Sonya is a 17 year old female who is presenting with complaints of infrequent periods. Menarche was 13 years of age. She has never been sexually active. She points out some discolouration on the back of her neck that she noticed a few months ago. On exam, she is well grown with a BMI of 29. She is Tanner stage 5 for breast and pubic hair development. Heart, lung and abdominal exam are benign aside from striae on her abdomen. She has acne on her back and face. Neurologic exam is normal. Blood work is pending. Most likely diagnosis based on the provided information?

options.html: Unable to say - need blood work

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The discolouration on the back of her neck is acanthosis nigricans, and it is the sign the stem is built around - velvety hyperpigmentation in the flexures, a marker of insulin resistance.

>

> Put beside it: infrequent periods (anovulation), BMI 29, acne on back and face (hyperandrogenism), fully developed at Tanner 5 so the axis works. That is the vault's PCOS clue list - ⭐ hirsutism, acne, obesity, and cycles irregular rather than absent - and PCOS is ⭐ the commonest secondary cause of amenorrhea at 28%.

>

> ⚠ B is the answer the question is testing you against. PCOS is a clinical diagnosis, and the Rotterdam pattern - irregular cycles plus clinical hyperandrogenism - is already satisfied by what is in front of you. Bloods confirm and exclude; they do not create the diagnosis.

>

> C would bring galactorrhea and a normal BMI, and the vault notes hyperprolactinemia is as often a drug as a tumour. D describes her metabolic risk, and the striae and acanthosis fit it, but ⚠ metabolic syndrome does not cause infrequent periods - it is the company PCOS keeps, not the diagnosis.

>

> Principle: anovulation plus clinical hyperandrogenism is PCOS before the bloods come back, and acanthosis names the mechanism.

stem: What is the underlying mechanism of amenorrhea in hyperprolactinemia?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ The key is B - prolactin inhibits the SECRETION of LH and FSH, and the discrimination the question is really testing is B against C: secretion, not production. The gonadotrophs still make the hormones; what fails is their pulsatile release. The source strikes C out for exactly that reason.

>

> Without LH and FSH pulses there is no follicular development, no estrogen, no ovulation and no menses.

>

> ⚠ ⭐ D is where the vault and this key pull apart, and it is worth knowing which is which. In-Class - Amenorrhea describes the chain as ↓ T4 → ↑ TRH → ↑ TSH and ↑ prolactin → prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses → anovulation - which is option D, the upstream trigger. The source's own annotation draws the same arrow, *GnRH ↓ → ↓ LH, FSH*. The quiz keys the proximate mechanism of the amenorrhea rather than the upstream cause of it. Both sentences are true; they answer different questions, and this one is keyed B.

>

> A is downstream of the gonadotropins, not the mechanism itself.

>

> Principle: prolactin silences GnRH, so gonadotropin SECRETION fails - and if a stem offers both links in that chain, read whether it is asking for the trigger or the mechanism.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Erika is 14 year old girl who you are seeing for amenorrhea. She has not yet started her period. She reports that she is previously healthy but is getting bullied in school because she hasn't started to “develop”. On exam, she is Tanner stage I for breast development and Tanner stage II for pubic hair. You note subtle dysmorphic features. Remainder of her exam is unremarkable. Her growth chart is shown.

stem: What is the most appropriate next test?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ FSH is the single number that splits the differential, and this stem and the next are deliberately a pair: this one asks what to do next, the next asks what makes the diagnosis.

>

> The vault puts it plainly: ⭐ high FSH means the ovary has failed; low FSH means the problem is above it.

>

> Erika's picture points hard at the ovarian column - Tanner I breast (no estrogen) with Tanner II pubic hair (adrenarche has happened, so the adrenal is fine), subtle dysmorphic features, and a growth chart. That is ⭐ Turner syndrome, the commonest cause of primary amenorrhea at 27%, whose clues are listed as short stature, webbed neck, shield chest.

>

> A and C belong to a short-stature workup, and would be reasonable if growth were the only issue - but she has absent puberty with dysmorphism, which is a different question. D measures the downstream consequence rather than the level that localises the lesion.

>

> Principle: in absent puberty, FSH first - it tells you whether to look at the ovary or above it.

preamble.html: Erika is 14 year old girl who you are seeing for amenorrhea. She has not yet started her period. She reports that she is previously healthy but is getting bullied in school because she hasn't started to “develop”. On exam, she is Tanner stage I for breast development and Tanner stage II for pubic hair. You note subtle dysmorphic features. Remainder of her exam is unremarkable. Her growth chart is shown.

stem: What is the most appropriate test for diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The previous question localised the lesion; this one names it. The vault's ovarian column gives the next test in one word: ⭐ karyotype - and the investigation list repeats it, ⭐ karyotype when FSH is high.

>

> That is what confirms Turner syndrome (45,X and its mosaics), and it also separates the two gonadal dysgeneses - ⭐ XY gonadal dysgenesis carries a malignancy risk and the gonads are excised, which is a management decision no hormone level can make for you.

>

> ⚠ B is the right answer to the question before it, and that is exactly the trap. FSH tells you the ovary has failed; it never tells you why. D would show a uterus - useful, but Erika's problem is absent development, not absent outflow. A dates the skeleton without diagnosing anything.

>

> Principle: FSH localises, karyotype diagnoses - and in Turner the karyotype also decides what happens to the gonads.

preamble.html: Jennifer is 16 year old female who presents with primary amenorrhea. She is previously healthy and has had no surgeries. She has been sexually active with her boyfriend but uses condoms. She occasionally drinks alcohol on the weekends and has experimented with Ecstasy. She is a B student. She exercises 6-7 days per week. On exam, she is Tanner stage V for breast and pubic hair. Exam is otherwise unremarkable. Growth chart is shown.

stem: The most important initial first test is:
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Rule out pregnancy first, before any other test and whatever the story sounds like. It is the top branch of the vault's flowchart and its first high-yield discriminator.

>

> ⚠ "Primary amenorrhea" makes this feel wrong, and that is the trap. Never having menstruated does not exclude pregnancy: ovulation precedes the first period, so conception is possible before menarche. She is sexually active, and condoms are a method with real typical-use failure.

>

> C is the number that splits the differential, but it comes after the hCG. D sits on the branch below FSH. A would answer whether she has a uterus, which her Tanner V development already makes likely.

>

> Principle: primary amenorrhea does not exempt a sexually active 16-year-old from a pregnancy test.

Once you have the result of your first test, it is normal and you need to do further testing.

stem: Which of the following will be most helpful in this context?

options.html: Serum FSH, LSH, prolactin, thyroid function
Serum FSH, LH, thyroid function, karyotype
Perform a pelvic ultrasound and pelvic exam

answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ In PRIMARY amenorrhea the second question is anatomy, not hormones. Pregnancy is excluded, so the next thing worth knowing is whether there is a uterus and whether blood can get out - and a pelvic examination with ultrasound answers both at once.

>

> The source annotates this exactly: *reproductive tract intact*, and beside it *structural, outflow abnormalities*. It also notes *no issue with FSH, LH* - her Tanner stage V development already tells you the axis has worked, which is what makes the hormonal panel the less informative test at this point.

>

> The numbers back it. ⭐ Mullerian agenesis (MRKH) is 15% of primary amenorrhea, and the outflow causes - imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum - are common in adolescents and present exactly at menarche. None of them shows up on a thyroid or prolactin level.

>

> ⚠ This is where a secondary-amenorrhea reflex misleads you. In a woman who used to menstruate, the prolactin and thyroid panel is the right second step, because the anatomy has already proved itself by working. In someone who has never menstruated, it has not.

>

> A is the androgen panel, for a patient with hyperandrogenic signs she does not have. C adds a karyotype before there is a high FSH to justify it.

>

> Principle: never menstruated means prove the plumbing first; used to menstruate means check the hormones first.

The correct answer is B.

>

> ⚠ The option contains a typo - “LSH” for LH - and it is the source's, circled in her own copy, reproduced here as written.

>

>

> Principle: FSH with prolactin and thyroid is the localising panel; the karyotype waits for a high FSH.

Serum FSH and LH are low. Genital exam is within normal limits. Karyotype and ultrasound are normal.

stem: Your next step is:

options.html: Perform a MRI of the head
Perform a MRI of the abdomen

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Low FSH and LH puts her in the ⭐ hypothalamic / hypogonadotropic column, and the vault's instruction for that column is unambiguous: ⭐ functional causes first, MRI only if no stressor - and its investigation list warns ⚠ MRI is not first line.

>

> She has an obvious stressor: she ⭐ exercises 6-7 days per week, which is the column's own named clue - low BMI, athlete, recent stressor. So the imaging that A proposes is precisely what the note says to hold back.

>

> The progesterone challenge is the right next move, and one of the CHSG's stated objectives is to know its indications. It answers whether there is enough estrogen to have primed an endometrium: a bleed means estrogen is present and the tract is patent; ⭐ no bleed points to a deeper hypoestrogenic state, which is what sustained energy deficit produces.

>

> ⚠ The OCR of this option dropped its letter - the source reads ) Perform a progesterone challenge. Transcribed as C from its position.

>

> D screens for late-onset CAH, which belongs on the anovulation branch and is already unlikely with normal androgens.

>

> Principle: low gonadotropins with a stressor in the history is functional until excluded - scan last, not first.

Serum FSH and LH are low. Genital exam is within normal limits. Karyotype and ultrasound are normal.

stem: The most likely diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is C.

Everything has been excluded except the thing that was in the social history from the start.

>

> | Finding | What it rules out |

> | --- | --- |

> | Low FSH and LH | ⭐ Turner - ovarian failure gives HIGH FSH |

> | Normal karyotype, normal genital exam | AIS, which is 46,XY with absent pubic hair |

> | Normal testosterone, DHEAS, 46,XX | CAH, which is hyperandrogenic |

> | Tanner V, normal ultrasound | an outflow or developmental cause |

>

> What remains is ⭐ functional hypothalamic amenorrhea - 15% of secondary amenorrhea, whose triggers the vault lists as eating disorder, exercise, stress. Exercising 6-7 days per week is the mechanism: sustained energy deficit shuts down GnRH pulses, so gonadotropins fall and the ovary is never asked to work.

>

> ⚠ The treatment is not hormonal first. The vault says ⭐ restore energy availability, with HRT only if it persists - and notes that ⭐ estrogen deficiency costs bone whatever the compartment, which is why this is not a benign diagnosis in a 16-year-old still building peak bone mass.

>

> Principle: low gonadotropins with a normal everything else and an athlete's history is functional - and the treatment is energy, not estrogen.

stem: At what Bhcg can a TV ultrasound detect a gestational sac?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ About 1500 mU/ml is the discriminatory zone - the level above which a normal intrauterine pregnancy should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound.

>

> That number is the hinge of the whole lecture, because it turns an empty uterus into information:

>

> - Bhcg above the zone with no intrauterine pregnancy → ⭐ high suspicion for an ectopic

> - Bhcg below it with no intrauterine pregnancy → a pregnancy of unknown location, which may simply be too early

>

> Put beside the deck's other numbers: serum Bhcg is negative below 5, it is about 100 at the missed period, about 1000 at 6 weeks, and it peaks near 100,000 at 10 weeks, ⭐ doubling every 1.4-2.1 days in a viable pregnancy.

>

> This is why Case 1 was so alarming: her Bhcg was 8962, far above the zone, and the uterus was empty.

>

> Principle: an empty uterus only means something once you know the Bhcg.

stem: What are you obliged to rule out when a patient with an iud has a positive pregnancy test?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

The deck states it as a rule to carry rather than a probability to weigh: ⭐ "IUD and a positive pregnancy test is an Ectopic until proven otherwise."

>

> The logic is about what the device does and does not prevent. An intrauterine device is very effective at preventing intrauterine implantation, so of the pregnancies that occur despite one, ⭐ a disproportionate share are outside the uterus. The absolute risk of ectopic is lowered; the proportion is raised.

>

> It sits beside the deck's companion rule: ⭐ "Abdo pain + bleeding + positive bhcg is an Ectopic until proven otherwise."

>

> A is what you hope to find and must still confirm, but it is not what you are obliged to exclude. B and D are on the differential without carrying the same duty.

>

> Principle: the device makes a pregnancy unlikely and an ectopic relatively likely - so a positive test with an IUD is an ectopic until imaged.

stem: Which is a contraindication to Methotrexate treatment in the setting of an Ectopic Pregnancy?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ A viable intrauterine pregnancy is an ABSOLUTE contraindication - methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist that inhibits DNA synthesis, so giving it to a wanted intrauterine pregnancy would be teratogenic or fatal to it. This matters because of heterotopic pregnancy, where an intrauterine and an ectopic pregnancy coexist.

>

> The deck's absolute list: breastfeeding · immunodeficiency · liver disease or alcoholism · blood dyscrasias · methotrexate sensitivity · acute pulmonary disease · peptic ulcer disease · renal dysfunction · Bhcg > 5000 · viable intrauterine pregnancy. ⭐ The relative list is short: fetal heart activity, and an ectopic mass > 4 cm.

>

> Every distractor is a near-miss against that list, and the numbers are the point:

>

> - B - ⚠ Bhcg 2000 is below the 5000 cutoff, so it is not a contraindication

> - D - ⚠ 2 cm is below the 4 cm mass, and that entry is only relative anyway

> - C - a corpus luteal cyst is an expected finding in early pregnancy

>

> Principle: learn the two numbers, 5000 and 4 cm, and note that one is absolute and the other only relative.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. A 27 yr old presents to urgent care with RLQ pain for 1 day.

stem: What else would you like to know?

options.html: Her LMP, any vaginal bleeding, contraception, and whether her shoulder hurts
Her appetite, bowel habit and whether the pain is worse after eating a fatty meal
Her urinary frequency, dysuria and whether she has any flank pain or fever at all
Her cervical screening history and whether she has ever had an abnormal pap test

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ The single most important question in a woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain is the LMP, because it decides whether a pregnancy test is needed - and the deck's whole thesis is that ⚠ a low threshold for ordering a Bhcg will prevent missing a pregnancy diagnosis.

>

> The deck's own history list: LMP · quality of pain, associated GI and GU symptoms, fever, appetite · sexually active, trying to conceive, contraception used · obstetrical history · shoulder tip pain, dizziness, any associated vaginal bleeding · history of PID · past medical, medications, allergies, past surgery, social history.

>

> ⭐ Shoulder tip pain is the one worth reaching for deliberately. It is referred pain from diaphragmatic irritation by blood in the peritoneum, so it is not a vague associated symptom - it is a sign of haemoperitoneum, and she has it.

>

> B, C and D are all reasonable in a general abdominal pain history and all of them miss the pregnancy.

>

> Principle: ask the LMP first, and ask about the shoulder deliberately - it is the question that finds blood in the abdomen.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. A 27 yr old presents to urgent care with RLQ pain for 1 day. LMP Aug 10, 2025, hx of irregular periods, missed Aug period, GA 6 wks 3 days, Gravida 1. Pain severe yesterday and then settled, worse again today, now 8/10 across lower abdomen, also pain in shoulder tip, feels like she has to have a bowel movement too but nothing there. Spotting since Sept 5, 2025. Vitals - HR 80, BP 120/70 lying; HR 100, BP 105/60 sitting. Abdomen soft, slightly distended, ? rebound. Hb 122, O positive blood, Bhcg 8962.

stem: Ultrasound - what kind is best?

options.html: Transabdominal, since it gives the widest view of the pelvis and the free fluid
Transvaginal, which is the more sensitive way to see an early pregnancy
CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast, to look for the site of bleeding
MRI of the pelvis, which avoids ionising radiation in a pregnant patient

answer:
The correct answer is B.

⭐ Transvaginal ultrasound, because the probe sits next to the structures of interest and resolves an early pregnancy that a transabdominal view would miss.

>

> It is also the route the deck's numbers assume: the ⭐ discriminatory zone of about 1500 mU/ml is a transvaginal threshold. Quoting it against a transabdominal scan would be wrong, since the transabdominal threshold is far higher.

>

> A is often done first and is not useless - it finds free fluid well - but it is not the best test for an early intrauterine pregnancy. C irradiates a pregnancy and answers a question ultrasound answers better. D is slow and unavailable in urgent care.

>

> Principle: the discriminatory zone is a transvaginal number, so the scan that goes with it is transvaginal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. A 27 yr old presents to urgent care with RLQ pain for 1 day. LMP Aug 10, 2025, hx of irregular periods, missed Aug period, GA 6 wks 3 days, Gravida 1. Pain severe yesterday and then settled, worse again today, now 8/10 across lower abdomen, also pain in shoulder tip, feels like she has to have a bowel movement too but nothing there. Spotting since Sept 5, 2025. Vitals - HR 80, BP 120/70 lying; HR 100, BP 105/60 sitting. Abdomen soft, slightly distended, ? rebound. Hb 122, O positive blood, Bhcg 8962.

stem: What information does that tell you?

options.html: The Bhcg is too low to interpret, so the scan should be deferred and repeated later
She is anemic and Rh negative, so she needs both transfusion and Rhogam urgently
She should have a visible intrauterine pregnancy, her Hb is adequate, and no Rhogam
The Bhcg is consistent with a pregnancy of unknown location, which needs no action

answer:
The correct answer is C.

Three numbers, three conclusions, and the deck draws all three:

>

> | Value | What it means |

> | --- | --- |

> | Bhcg 8962 | ⭐ far above the ~1500 discriminatory zone - we should be able to see a normal intrauterine pregnancy |

> | Hb 122 | ⭐ okay at the moment - and "at the moment" is the operative phrase |

> | O positive | ⭐ she does not need Rhogam, since she is Rh positive |

>

> ⚠ The Hb conclusion has a short shelf life, which is the lesson. It was 122 at 10:51; by 17:07 it was 105. A reassuring haemoglobin in a bleeding patient is a snapshot, not a verdict.

>

> D inverts the definition: ⭐ a pregnancy of unknown location is the situation when the Bhcg is BELOW the zone, where an empty uterus may just be early. Above the zone, an empty uterus is a finding.

>

> Principle: the Bhcg tells you what the scan should show, the Hb tells you where she is right now, and the blood group tells you whether to give Rhogam.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. A 27 yr old presents to urgent care with RLQ pain for 1 day. LMP Aug 10, 2025, hx of irregular periods, missed Aug period, GA 6 wks 3 days, Gravida 1. Pain severe yesterday and then settled, worse again today, now 8/10 across lower abdomen, also pain in shoulder tip, feels like she has to have a bowel movement too but nothing there. Spotting since Sept 5, 2025. Vitals - HR 80, BP 120/70 lying; HR 100, BP 105/60 sitting. Abdomen soft, slightly distended, ? rebound. Hb 122, O positive blood, Bhcg 8962. Ultrasound shows what looks like a yolk sac in the adnexa, no intrauterine pregnancy, a fetal heart beating at 125 bpm in the adnexal mass, and hemoperitoneum. She is transferred, and a repeat Hb is 105.

stem: Does anyone know what it is called when there is an intrauterine pregnancy and a pregnancy outside the uterus?

options.html: A molar pregnancy with a coexistent fetus

answer:
The correct answer is A.

⭐ Heterotopic pregnancy - an intrauterine and an extrauterine pregnancy at the same time.

>

> It matters far out of proportion to how rare it is, because ⚠ it breaks the rule everyone leans on. Seeing an intrauterine pregnancy normally reassures you that there is no ectopic; in a heterotopic pregnancy that reasoning fails, and the ectopic is found late. It is commoner after assisted reproduction.

>

> It is also why ⭐ a viable intrauterine pregnancy is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate - the drug would destroy the wanted pregnancy along with the ectopic.

>

> B is a location of ectopic, within the cornual part of the tube, and a dangerous one - not a coexisting pair. C is an empty uterus with a Bhcg below the zone. D is a different entity entirely.

>

> Principle: an intrauterine pregnancy usually excludes an ectopic, and heterotopic is the exception that kills people.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. A 27 yr old presents to urgent care with RLQ pain for 1 day. LMP Aug 10, 2025, hx of irregular periods, missed Aug period, GA 6 wks 3 days, Gravida 1. Pain severe yesterday and then settled, worse again today, now 8/10 across lower abdomen, also pain in shoulder tip, feels like she has to have a bowel movement too but nothing there. Spotting since Sept 5, 2025. Vitals - HR 80, BP 120/70 lying; HR 100, BP 105/60 sitting. Abdomen soft, slightly distended, ? rebound. Hb 122, O positive blood, Bhcg 8962. Ultrasound shows what looks like a yolk sac in the adnexa, no intrauterine pregnancy, a fetal heart beating at 125 bpm in the adnexal mass, and hemoperitoneum. She is transferred, and a repeat Hb is 105.

stem: What is best treatment for this patient? Expectant, medical or surgical and why?

options.html: Expectant, since her pain has settled once already and her vitals are stable
Medical with methotrexate, since she is haemodynamically stable on arrival
Either medical or expectant, decided by her own preference after counselling
Surgical - her Bhcg is over 5000, her Hb is falling and there is blood

answer:
The correct answer is D.

⭐ Surgery, and the deck lists four independent reasons, any one of which would be enough:

>

> - Bhcg > 5000 - an absolute contraindication to methotrexate

> - Hb dropping - 122 at 10:51, 105 at 17:07

> - Hemoperitoneum - she is bleeding into her abdomen now

> - In pain

>

> Measure her against the deck's expectant criteria and she fails almost all of them: those require asymptomatic, no evidence of hemoperitoneum, and ⭐ a Bhcg ≤ 200 and decreasing. Hers is 8962 and she is symptomatic.

>

> ⚠ She also has fetal cardiac activity at 125 bpm, which is both a relative contraindication to methotrexate and an indication for surgery on the deck's own list - and her orthostatic vitals (120/70 lying, 105/60 sitting with a pulse of 100) are early haemodynamic compromise.

>

> Principle: methotrexate has a ceiling at Bhcg 5000, and a falling haemoglobin with hemoperitoneum is an operation, not a decision.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. At surgery a salpingotomy was attempted, and the tube was opened to remove the tubal pregnancy.

stem: If a salpingotomy (also known as salpingostomy) was performed are there any special tests to be done post op? What are the risks of leaving the tube behind?

options.html: No specific follow-up is needed once the pregnancy has been removed from the tube
A repeat ultrasound at six weeks, to confirm the tube has healed without a stricture
Serial Bhcg until it reaches zero, since trophoblast can persist in the tube
A hysterosalpingogram before any future pregnancy, to confirm the tube is patent

answer:
The correct answer is C.

⭐ Salpingotomy opens the tube and leaves it behind, so the operation is not necessarily the end of the pregnancy. Trophoblastic tissue can remain in the retained tube and keep producing Bhcg - persistent trophoblast - so the Bhcg is followed serially until it is undetectable, and methotrexate is given if it plateaus or rises.

>

> ⭐ This is the whole difference between the two operations. A salpingectomy removes the tube and the problem with it; a salpingotomy preserves the tube for future fertility and buys that with follow-up and risk:

>

> - Persistent trophoblast, needing methotrexate or further surgery

> - ⚠ A damaged tube is itself a risk factor for a future ectopic, so the tube that was saved may be the site of the next one

>

> In this case the salpingotomy failed because of increased bleeding, so a salpingectomy was performed, which controlled it - and she went home the same day.

>

> Principle: if you leave the tube, you follow the Bhcg to zero - and you accept a tube that may host the next ectopic.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 2. A 34 yr old female G2P1, previously healthy, presents May 27 with RLQ pain 10/10 a few days ago, now decreased. Spotting for 5 days. LMP Apr 20, on time, hx q28 day cycles. OB hx SVD. Smoker. Vitals stable, Hb 132, AB positive, BHCG 684. Ultrasound shows a right adnexal possible gestational sac c/w 5 wks GA, no hemoperitoneum, no intrauterine pregnancy, possible ectopic. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no peritoneal signs.

stem: Management options? Expectant vs Methotrexate vs Surgery. What do you recommend?

options.html: Surgery, since any possible ectopic with a positive Bhcg needs the tube removed
Methotrexate - she is stable, unruptured, and her Bhcg is well under 5000
Expectant management, since she is comfortable and her ultrasound is equivocal
Repeat the Bhcg in a week, and decide only if the ultrasound findings progress

answer:
The correct answer is B.

She meets every methotrexate criterion the deck lists: ⭐ high suspicion for ectopic · haemodynamically stable · not ruptured, with no free fluid · able to comply with follow-up - and her Bhcg of 684 is well below the 5000 ceiling with a 2 cm mass, under the 4 cm relative limit.

>

> ⚠ ⭐ And she does NOT meet the expectant criteria, which is the most useful thing in this case. Those require a Bhcg ≤ 200 and decreasing; hers is 684, and on follow-up it rose to 1112, then 1438.

>

> What actually happened is the teaching point. After counselling she chose expectant management, and it was honoured - the deck records the safety-netting carefully: repeat Bhcg in 2-3 days, return for abdominal pain, dizziness or shoulder tip pain, ⭐ do not go anywhere remote and do not be alone. Her Bhcg rose twice, she took methotrexate on Jun 4, it produced only a 14% drop against the 15% target from day 4 to day 7, and on Jun 21 she presented with moderate hemoperitoneum and had a laparoscopic right salpingectomy. She did well.

>

> ⚠ So the recommended answer and the patient's choice differed, and the case follows the choice. That is a real consultation, not a failure - but the criteria are what the exam will ask for.

>

> Principle: expectant management needs a Bhcg under 200 and falling; anything rising is at best a methotrexate case.

stem: Which of the following statements about breast cancer is true?

options.html: Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women
20% of breast cancers are due to an underlying hereditary BRCA mutation
20% of invasive breast cancers are classified pathologically as "no special type"
Paget’s disease of the nipple is due to the presence of carcinoma cells in the squamous epithelium of the nipple
20% of breast cancers are considered to be sporadic

answer: The correct answer is D. While breast cancer is the most common cancer in Canadian women, it is not the leading cause of cancer death in Canadian women; therefore selection a) is incorrect. While 20% of breast cancers are non-sporadic/familial/hereditary, not all non-sporadic/familial/hereditary breast cancers are due to an inherited mutation in the BRCA gene; therefore selection b) is incorrect. Most (80%) of invasive breast cancers are classified pathologically as invasive mammary carcinoma of no special type; therefore selection c) is incorrect. Most (80%) of breast cancers are considered to be sporadic; therefore selection e) is incorrect.

stem: Which of the following statements defines small for gestational age (SGA)?

options.html: Birth weight less than the 10th percentile
Birth prior to 35 weeks gestational age

answer: The correct answer is B. Small for gestational age is defined as a birth weight less than the 10th percentile for a given gestational age, and as such is not defined by a specific weight number or week of gestation. The actual birth weight will determine if the fetus is extremely low birth weight/low birthweight, which may have implications for risk of long term health problems, but a baby may be extremely low birth weight (ie 800g) but still a very appropriate weight, or even large for gestational age if the delivery was extremely premature (ie 23-24 weeks). A birth at 35 weeks would be considered premature, but the gestational age alone does not in and of itself confirm that a baby is growth restricted or SGA.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following is a risk factor for intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
answer: The correct answer is D. IUGR can be caused by many factors, and often a combination of factors. Medical conditions such as hypertension can lead to microvascular damage within the placenta as it may disrupt the capillary vessels providing oxygen and nutrition exchange at the maternal/placental interface. Chromosomal anomalies often result in improper or limited cell division and duplication resulting in reduce mass of developing organs and tissues, thus may predispose to IUGR developing. As well, if the chromosomal anomaly is also within the placenta it may impact proper placental implantation and functioning resulting in overall poor fetal growth. Hyperthyroidism may lead to increased metabolic demands which may result in poor overall fetal growth due to consumption of metabolic resources, but hypothyroidism does not impact fetal growth typically.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following is an INTRINSIC cause of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)?
answer: The correct answer is B. Intrinsic causes of IUGR imply problems arising directly with fetal tissue growth as opposed to imposed on the fetus due to a lack of nutrient delivery. Genetic abnormalities such as trisomy 21 may impact growth due to direct problems with cell duplication secondary to the abnormal chromosomal compliment. Smoking and hypertension may both lead to microvascular damage in the placenta thus restricting nutrient delivery. Multiple gestations often result in IUGR relative to gestational age equivalent singleton pregnancies but to a limited nutrient delivery from the maternal circulation.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following ultrasound findings are likely to be seen in a baby with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) less than the 3rd percentile due to placental insufficiency?

options.html: Absent end diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler

answer: The correct answer is C. In the setting of severe placental insufficiency, the primary problem is a reduced capacity to circulate blood within the placenta due to microvascular damage at the capillary level. As a result of this, the fetal cardiovascular system has to work harder to flow blood through the more limited placental circulation resulting in increased resistance to flow (an increased resistive index or pulsatility index). As the microvascular damage becomes more severe and thus it becomes harder to circulate blood through the placenta, Doppler ultrasound findings may progress to the point of showing absent end diastolic flow (AEDF) where the flow of blood through the umbilical cord momentarily pauses at the endo of the cardiac cycle while the ventricles are refilling for the next beat. This is because the resistance to flow within the placenta is so significant that it requires a positive pushing force from the fetal heart to maintain forward movement into the placenta. In a setting of severe placental insufficiency and IUGR, fetal nutritional delivery is typically compromised and will lead to reduced fetal renal circulation and thus a reduction in amniotic fluid volume. Vasa previa alone is not typically associated with IUGR.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Which of the following definitions of high blood pressure in pregnancy BEST defines gestational hypertension?
answer: The correct answer is B. Looking at the definitions of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, gestational hypertension is defined as a new onset blood pressure problem developing after 20 weeks gestation. The normal physiologic changes in pregnancy typically result in a reduction in blood pressure in the first trimester and early second trimester, as the blood volume is beginning to increase but the systemic vascular resistance is dropping at a greater rate/percentage meaning that the actual blood pressure is lower until the blood volume capacity catches up to the capacity of the vascular system. Thus if the BP is elevated in the early stages of pregnancy it likely represents a preexisting/chronic hypertension issue that has been diagnosed in pregnancy due to the seeking of prenatal care.

The 2026 Schmidt deck (12 - Hypertension in Pregnancy) also defines gestational hypertension as onset after 20 weeks, which is option C. Transcribed as keyed, flagged not corrected.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Which of the following statements regarding preeclampsia is TRUE?

options.html: Requires a systolic blood pressure >160mmHg to diagnose
Is caused by human placental lactogen
Most commonly develops before 20 weeks gestation

answer: The correct answer is E. Preeclampsia is a complex medical condition which is not fully understood in terms of its causes/mechanisms of action. It classically develops in primagravidas at the end of pregnancy (beyond 36 weeks), but may develop in any pregnancy regardless of parity. Hypertension is defined as a systolic BP >140 or diastolic BP > 90. If the systolic pressure is >160 this is considered severe hypertension and carries a higher risk of developing sequela, thus indicating a more urgent need to consider treatment. Human placental lactogen is a hormone produced by the placenta which interferes with the normal maternal management of glucose, and is associated with the development of gestational diabetes.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Which of the following conditions may predispose to developing preeclampsia?
answer: The correct answer is E. Molar pregnancies are due to an abnormal chromosome complement: A partial molar pregnancy with 69 chromosomes due to the egg being fertilized simultaneously with 2 sperm, or a sperm/egg which did not properly undergo meiosis resulting in a complement of 46 chromosomes rather than 23, or a complete mole resulting from fertilization of an empty egg (no maternal genetic material) with a sperm containing 46 paternal chromosomes/2 sperm simultaneously. Molar pregnancies typically have extremely high bHCG levels (sometime into the millions, compared to a normal peak level of 100,000-200,000), which can lead to severe blood pressure problems and early onset preeclampsia due to a heightened response to circulating vasoactive substances. Smoking has been shown to slightly reduce the likelihood of developing preeclampsia, although significantly increases the risk of developing other pregnancy complications such as IUGR and placental insufficiency. Hypothyroidism typically does not have an impact on BP, however hyperthyroidism may lead to BP abnormalities and thyroid storm if not treated.

flags.title: The module's key contradicts its own rationale
flags.html: The Rise module keys E, "A, B and C", but its rationale says "smoking has been shown to slightly reduce the likelihood of developing preeclampsia" and "hypothyroidism typically does not have an impact on BP". Only A, molar pregnancy, survives the module's own reasoning. Transcribed as keyed, flagged not corrected.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Which of the following medications for the management of hypertension is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is D. Beta blockers such as labetalol, alpha blockers such as methyldopa and calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine are all safe and effective medications in pregnancy to control BP. The normal physiologic changes in pregnancy lead to an increase in blood volume, particularly the fluid component which can limit the effectiveness of diuretic agents such as methyldopa. As a result diuretics are not optimal medications to use and ideally should be switched to another medication category, but are not inherently unsafe to use. ACE inhibitors have been associated with fetal teratogenic effects and in the mid to later stages of pregnancy can lead to fetal renal damage and as such should not be used in pregnancy. Ideally in women planning a pregnancy they would be switched to an alternative medication before conception to ensure that BP management is normal and stable before becoming pregnant rather than switched during pregnancy so severe BP problems that may arise during the transition can be avoided.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lecture: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Signs and symptoms of pregnancy: Which of the following are common signs/symptoms of pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is D. The hormonal changes of pregnancy often induce a feeling of nausea in many pregnant women due to the rapid rise of the bHCG level in the first trimester. Amenorrhea is typical as the bHCG leads to the persistence of the corpus luteum which prevents the hormonal cascade that induces menses, allowing the further placental development to maintain hormonal profiles that will allow the pregnancy to continue on. Most women will experience more urinary frequency and volume due to the increased blood volume developing during early pregnancy, in conjunction with increased glomerular filtration rate and thus increased urine volume.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lecture: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Uterine growth: At which gestational age does the measurement of the symphysis-fundus height (SFH) in centimeters begin to match with the gestational age in weeks?
answer: The correct answer is B. As pregnancy progresses the uterus will grow in size in typical patterns and as such can generally be identified at several points in the pelvis/abdomen over the course of pregnancy. The fundus of the uterus is typically palpable at the symphysis pubis at 12 weeks gestation. By 20 weeks the fundus is usually at the umbilicus, and this location with fairly consistently match up with a measurement from the symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus of 20cm. From this stage on in pregnancy, the SFH will generally match in centimeters the gestational age in weeks.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lecture: Care for Pregnancy in the First Trimester
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: First trimester investigations: Which of the following investigations are NOT part of the routine recommended antenatal bloodwork in the first trimester?
answer: The correct answer is A. Routine antenatal blood work should ideally be drawn in the early stages of pregnancy to ensure that there are no abnormal results that can direct treatment or management (ie severe anemia, presence of antibodies, positive infectious disease screening). The recommended public health tests of VDRL (syphilis), hepatitis B, and HIV are all indicated as treatments are available and safe to use in pregnancy. HSV testing is not recommended routinely in pregnancy as the presence of antibodies alone does not determine if there is an increased risk of infection/transmission to the fetus. Investigation and treatment is typically only indicated in the setting of an acute infection with vaginal/perineal lesions to guide delivery management.
