weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Nutritional requirements: Which of the following supplements is commonly required during pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is B. Iron is required in significant amounts for the development of fetal red blood cells, as well as the significant increase in maternal red blood cells and uterine muscle tissue during pregnancy. Many women’s diets are inadequate to provide these increased needs and thus supplementation is strongly suggested. Vitamin E, vitamin D and manganese are less critically needed for the developing fetus and are typically adequately supplied in standard diets. Local mineral/vitamin deficiencies may affect this however, particularly in underdeveloped countries.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Vaccination in pregnancy: Which of the following vaccines are CONTRAINDICATED to administer during pregnancy?
answer: The correct answer is C. Most vaccines are safe to administer during pregnancy, the exception being live-attenuated vaccines. These types of vaccines use the intact organism which has been killed or neutralized in some fashion to neutralize it as a risk of causing active infection. In scenarios where this attenuation process may have been improperly performed, there becomes a risk that the vaccination process may in fact erroneously lead to active infection with the still live organism. Due to this theoretical risk, such vaccine formulations should not be given during pregnancy to protect the fetus from an inadvertent exposure. The MMR vaccine is a live-attenuated vaccine, the pertussis, influenza and hepatitis A vaccines are not.

weekLabel: Week 5 - Pregnancy: Fertility, Genetics, Antenatal Care & Hypertension
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (3 questions). Delivered in Asynch W5.
stem: Rh sensitization/immunoglobulin: Which of the following may lead to the development of a maternal antibody response?
answer: The correct answer is E. Rh sensitization commonly develops when fetal red blood cells leak across the placental interface into the maternal blood stream and provoke a maternal antibody response. Amniocentesis, involving passing a needle through the maternal abdomen and uterine wall into the amniotic fluid, may increase the risk of blood passing into the maternal circulation by disrupting the interface. Other possible sources of antibody development can be from a blood transfusion leading to exposure to antigens not native to the maternal circulation, as well as IV drug use with shared needles that may contain blood from previous users.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (6 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following statements best describes bleeding due to a placenta previa?

options.html: Typically associated with a tender, firm uterus

answer: The correct answer is B. Bleeding in pregnancy due to a placenta previa typically is painless, as it often results from the subtle softening and dilating that occurs in the cervix due to uterine stretching as the baby is growing. This disrupts the placental/uterine interface at the level of the cervix resulting in vaginal bleeding which may range from very mild to life threatening. In contrast, bleeding due to a placental abruption usually occurs in the setting of painful, firm uterus as the disruption of the placenta and resulting blood collecting within the uterine cavity is a potent irritant to the uterus. Placenta previa is diagnosed by ultrasound confirmation of a placenta covering the cervix (complete previa) or a placental edge inserting within 2cm of the internal cervical os (a partial/marginal previa). While a placental abruption may show a collection of blood within the uterine cavity, in many cases the disruption at the placental edge results in the bleeding draining out of the uterine cavity through the cervix thus not showing any obvious signs on ultrasound, and as such in many cases abruption becomes a diagnosis of exclusion once other potential causes of vaginal bleeding have been ruled out.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (6 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following ultrasound findings indicate a placenta previa?

options.html: Placental edge covering the internal cervical os
Placental edge 4cm from the internal cervical os
Placental tissue visualized in a multi-lobed pattern

answer: The correct answer is A. A complete placenta previa is diagnosed when the placenta is implanted overtop of the internal cervical os, while a partial/marginal previa is diagnosed when the placental edge is implanted within 2cm of the internal cervical os. A bilobed placenta, or a succenturiate lobe (where a portion of the placenta implants separately from the main body of the placenta but connected to it by fetal blood vessels within the placental masses) can occur regardless of the location of the placenta and are not indicative of a previa. The presence of a velamentous cord can occur regardless of the placental location relative to the cervix as well. A velamentous cord insertion or bilobed placenta/succenturiate lobe can be associated with a vasa previa (presence of fetal blood vessels covering the internal cervical os or with 2cm of the os) if the placenta happens to be implanted lower in the uterus.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (6 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: Which of the following tests is most helpful in diagnosing bleeding due to a vasa previa?

options.html: History of a previous cesarean section

answer: The correct answer is D. When trying to differentiate the cause of vaginal bleeding, several investigations may be helpful in determining the source. Due to differences in the makeup of fetal hemoglobin compared to adult hemoglobin, the two can be differentiated. The Kleihauer-Betke test looks for the presence of fetal blood cells in the maternal circulation. This is indicative of a fetal-maternal hemorrhage (fetal cells leaking across the placental interface into the maternal bloodstream) and can be seen in cases of abdominal trauma, or occasionally in settings of a placental abruption. A previous cesarean section can a risk factor for the development of a placenta previa, but not vasa previa. Fetal bleeding with not have a direct impact on the maternal coagulation profile - the presence of severe maternal bleeding due to a placenta previa or placental abruption may lead to abnormalities in the coagulation profile however. The Apts test, similar to the Kleihauer-Betke test, looks for the presence of fetal blood cells in vaginal blood - a positive test indicates a fetal source of the blood and is indicative of a vasa previa.

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (6 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: A patient presents to Labour and Delivery triage at approximately 28 weeks gestation with no previous antenatal care. She complains of vaginal bleeding. She has filled a pad over the past two hours. She denies pain or contractions at this time. Which of the following would NOT be part of the next steps in the work-up?

options.html: Further history to identify patient risk factors, including previous history of bleeding, trauma, cigarette and cocaine use
An abdominal exam to assess for uterine tenderness and fetal presentation
A cervical examination to assess for dilatation
Bloodwork including a CBC, Group and Screen, and INR/PTT/fibrinogen

answer: The correct answer is C. Further history to identify patient risk factors, including previous history of bleeding, trauma, cigarette and cocaine use (these questions are all relevant to the work-up for antepartum hemorrhage) An abdominal exam to assess for uterine tenderness and fetal presentation (this is part of the routine work-up for antepartum hemorrhage) A cervical examination to assess for dilatation (The cervix should not be examined unless an ultrasound has shown the placenta to be "clear" ie not a placenta previa. Examining a patient with placenta previa in this way could lead to significant hemorrhage) Bloodwork including a CBC, Group and Screen, and INR/PTT/fibrinogen (this is part of the initial work-up of a patient presenting with bleeding. If the suspicion of feto-maternal hemorrhage is high, a Kleihaur Betke test can be ordered to assess this.)

weekLabel: Week 6 - Labour, Delivery, the Puerperium & the Newborn
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (6 questions). Delivered in Asynch W6.
stem: A patient presents to Labour and Delivery triage at 34 weeks complaining of constant abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She has filled 2 pads in the past hour. On examination, the uterus is tender to palpation and there is bright red blood coming from the cervix on speculum examination. The fetal heart rate is currently normal. Based on the information you have so far, which diagnosis is highest on your differential?
answer: The correct answer is D. Placenta previa (this typically presents with painless vaginal bleeding) Vasa previa (this may present with painless bleeding - bleeding in vasa previa is fetal in origin) Preterm labour (while the patient may be entering preterm labour at this time, the constant pain and significant bleeding is likely to represent placental abruption) Placental abruption (this is correct - placental abruption presents with painful vaginal bleeding. The fetal heart rate may initially be normal.)

stem: Cindy is a 28yo G1 who is found to have preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 28 weeks gestation. Upon assessment in triage, her cervix is 1cm dilated and she is not having regular contractions. She is afebrile and the fetal heart rate is normal. The Obstetrical team decides to admit her to hospital for monitoring and management. Which of the following would be part of the initial management of this patient? Check all that apply:

options.html: Antibiotics to increase the latency time between PPROM and birth

answer: The correct answers are A and E. Antenatal corticosteroids (correct - these are important for promoting fetal lung maturity in the case of a potential preterm birth) Magnesium sulfate (incorrect - while important for fetal neuroprotection if birth is imminent, this short acting medication is not indicated in a patient who is currently stable and not at risk of imminent birth) Penicillin G (incorrect - while important for Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis at the time of delivery, this medication is not indicated in a patient who is currently stable and not at risk of imminent birth) Indomethicin for tocolysis (incorrect - this medication can be used in an attempt to temporarily slow down or stop contractions to facilitate transfer to another centre or to give corticosteroids. Cindy is not currently contracting so this medication is not indicated at this time) Antibiotics to increase the latency time between PPROM and birth (correct - several different antibiotic protocols have been demonstrated to increase the chances of pregnancy prolongation by at least one week) Cervical cerclage (incorrect - this is a surgical procedure to decrease the risk of preterm birth related to "cervical insufficiency". It is indicated in cases of multiple previous second trimester pregnancy losses or when the cervix is found to be progressively shortening on ultrasound prior to 24 weeks gestation. It would not be indicated in this case with ruptured membranes at 28 weeks gestation)

lecture: Deck Case - Clinical Approach to Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Clinical Approach to Menopause deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 22 and 19, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 53 year old presents to your clinic with menopause concerns. You take a history focused on her menses, her symptoms, and contraindications to menopausal hormone therapy (MHT).

stem: Which of the following items in her history is a contraindication to MHT?

options.html: Hot flashes and night sweats that wake her most nights of the week
A previous blood clot in her leg, treated with anticoagulation
Vaginal dryness with pain during penetrative sexual intercourse
A last menstrual period that was about fourteen months ago

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slide 22 lists the contraindications to ask about as "blood clot, breast cancer history", and the deck's contraindication table (slide 19) lists "Active or history of venous thromboembolism" against estrogen - a history is enough, not only an active clot.

  • A is the indication, not a contraindication: estrogen is the gold standard for VMS (75% reduction, slide 16).
  • C is genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which is treated (lubricants, moisturizers, then vaginal estrogen), not a bar to treatment.
  • D simply dates her menopause (amenorrhea x 12 months, slide 3); MHT can be started safely under 60 and < 10 years post menopause with no contraindications.

lecture: Deck Case - Clinical Approach to Menopause
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Clinical Approach to Menopause deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is the deck's own, verbatim. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 53 year old presents to your clinic with menopause concerns. History covers her menses (LMP, regularity, heaviness, intermenstrual spotting), symptoms (hot flashes, sleep, mood, GSM, libido) and contraindications to MHT. You move on to the physical exam.

stem: Does this patient need a Pap? An endometrial biopsy?

options.html: Both, routinely, before any menopausal hormone therapy is started
An endometrial biopsy routinely at her age, and a Pap only if symptomatic
A Pap on schedule, and a biopsy only if her bleeding is abnormal
Neither, since cervical screening and endometrial sampling end at menopause

answer:
Reasoned answer (mine, not the deck's): C. The deck asks the question and never answers it; it turns on the menses history the slide has just told you to take, which is why that history comes first.

  • Pap: cervical screening is for asymptomatic people with a cervix, from about age 25, every 3 years on a normal result (06 - Cervical Cancer Screening). Nothing about menopause changes her place on that schedule.
  • Endometrial biopsy: it follows abnormal bleeding - every patient over 40 with AUB (15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding) and any postmenopausal bleeding (05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding). Without bleeding, ⚠ endometrial sampling should NOT be routinely performed (same note). Hence the history question about intermenstrual spotting.
  • B misapplies the over-40 rule, which is a rule about AUB, not about age. A is not in any of the block's notes. D: the notes give no age at which cervical screening stops, so that point is left open, but nothing in them ends it at menopause.

Settle it against the lecturer if the question comes up in class; the deck gives no answer of its own.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 53 year old presents to your clinic with menopause concerns. On history she reports vaginal dryness, burning and pain with intercourse.

stem: On physical exam, why should her vulva be examined?

options.html: To exclude a skin condition before attributing her symptoms to GSM
To measure the vaginal pH, which on its own confirms a diagnosis of GSM
To take an endometrial sample during the same pelvic examination
To decide whether she needs systemic rather than vaginal estrogen

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slide 22: "Examine the vulva if patient has GSM symptoms to r/o skin conditions." The note's older version names the vulvar conditions to look for - lichen sclerosus and atrophic vaginitis.

  • B: a pH > 5.0 is one of the deck's signs of GSM (slide 7), alongside pallor, loss of labial volume and pubic hair, introital stenosis and a thin vestibule - but it is one sign among several and the deck never calls it diagnostic on its own.
  • C: an endometrial biopsy is a separate question on the same slide, driven by bleeding, not by GSM.
  • D: GSM is treated locally (lubricants, moisturizers, then vaginal estrogen, DHEA or oral ospemifene, slide 13); the exam does not choose systemic therapy.

lecture: Module Case - Clinical Approach to Menopause: Ms. Thomas
lectureMeta: Case from the Clinical Approach to Menopause Elentra module, added 2026-09-27. The stem is the module's own, verbatim; its question is open-ended, so the options are written for this vault. Keyed from the module's reveal slides, whose answer is quoted.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ms. Thomas is a healthy 49yo woman who presents to her family doctor for annual check-up. She has noticed a 15lb weight gain over the past year. Her last menses was 8 months ago and she has mild hot flashes.

stem: What topics might you discuss at this appointment?

options.html: Starting systemic estrogen today, and an endometrial biopsy for the eight months of amenorrhea
Serum FSH to confirm menopause, a thyroid panel, and a referral for weight-loss medication
Diet, exercise, cutting caffeine, alcohol and smoking, calcium and vitamin D, and cooling
Reassurance only, since mild hot flashes and weight gain at 49 need no discussion yet

answer:
The correct answer is C. The module's answer: "Dietary recommendations · Regular exercise · Reduction of exacerbating factors - caffeine/alcohol, smoking · Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation · Cooling strategies - air conditioning/fans, loose clothing."

The reasoning below is mine, from 03 - Clinical Approach to Menopause:

  • ⭐ Eight months without a period is not yet menopause - that needs amenorrhea x 12 months - so she is in the perimenopause, with mild symptoms. Lifestyle is where this visit starts. The lecture's numbers: calcium 1200 mg · vitamin D 800 IU · sodium < 1300 mg, weight loss may help, avoid triggers, cool down.
  • ⚠ Exercise is here for her weight and general health, not her flashes - the deck says exercise and yoga are healthy but not recommended for VMS specifically.
  • A: mild flashes do not call for MHT yet, and ⚠ amenorrhea is not abnormal bleeding - an endometrial biopsy follows bleeding, not its absence.
  • B: menopause is a clinical diagnosis; FSH belongs to the workup of POI under 40, not a healthy 49-year-old.
  • D: the annual visit is exactly when the weight gain and the three post-menopausal risks (CVD, cancer, osteoporotic fracture) are worth raising.

lectureMeta: Case from the Clinical Approach to Menopause Elentra module, added 2026-09-27. The stem is the module's own, verbatim; its question is open-ended, so the options are written for this vault. Keyed from the module's reveal slides, whose answer is quoted.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ms. Thomas returns 6 months later. She is now 50 years old and returns with worsening hot flashes that impair her ability to function as a kindergarten teacher. She wants to try HRT but is scared because her cousin had endometrial cancer.

stem: Is she a candidate for HRT?

options.html: No, because a relative's endometrial cancer is a contraindication to estrogen
No, not until she has first failed a trial of an SSRI or of gabapentin for her flashes
Only vaginal estrogen, since systemic therapy is not started in the perimenopause
Yes, at 50 and within ten years of menopause with no contraindication to estrogen

answer:
The correct answer is D. The module's answer: "YES!"

The reasoning below is mine, from 03 - Clinical Approach to Menopause:

  • Her LMP is now 14 months back, so she is menopausal, and her VMS are now impairing her work - the indication. ⭐ MHT can be safely started with no contraindications, younger than 60 and < 10 years post menopause, and she is all three. Estrogen is the gold standard for VMS (75% reduction).
  • A: the contraindication list is about her own history - known, suspected or history of an estrogen-dependent cancer (endometrial, ovarian). A cousin's cancer is not on it.
  • B: non-hormonal drugs are for women who cannot or will not take estrogen; nothing requires failing them first.
  • C: ⚠ vaginal estrogen treats GSM, not VMS - it has no systemic absorption, so it would not touch her flashes.

lecture: Module Case - Clinical Approach to Menopause: Ms. Thomas
lectureMeta: Case from the Clinical Approach to Menopause Elentra module, added 2026-09-27. The stem is the module's own, verbatim; its question is open-ended, so the options are written for this vault. Keyed from the module's reveal slides, whose answer is quoted.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ms. Thomas, 50, has hot flashes that impair her work as a kindergarten teacher. She wants to try HRT but is scared because her cousin had endometrial cancer.

stem: What could you say to alleviate her concern about endometrial cancer?

options.html: Add a progestogen to protect the uterus, use the lowest dose, and reassess every year
Use estrogen alone, since it is the progestogen that raises the endometrial cancer risk
Choose transdermal estrogen, since skipping first-pass metabolism removes the uterine risk
Plan a routine endometrial biopsy every year for as long as she stays on hormone therapy

answer:
The correct answer is A. The module's answer: "Concurrent use of progestogen to protect the uterus from the estrogen · Use lowest dose possible · Will reassess annually to decide when to discontinue use."

The reasoning below is mine, from 03 - Clinical Approach to Menopause:

  • ⭐ If she has a uterus, she needs progesterone - it is there to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. The endometrial risk belongs to estrogen-only regimens, which is why B is backwards: estrogen alone is for women who have had a hysterectomy.
  • C: transdermal estrogen's advantage is the clotting profile; it is still estrogen reaching the endometrium.
  • D: the endometrium is evaluated for bleeding - after 6 months of continuous MHT, after a spell of amenorrhea on it, or abnormal bleeding on cyclic MHT - not on a routine schedule.
  • Outside the block's notes: a cousin is a distant relative; a family pattern of endometrial and colorectal cancer would raise Lynch syndrome, which is a separate conversation from MHT.

lectureMeta: Case from the Clinical Approach to Menopause Elentra module, added 2026-09-27. The stem is the module's own, verbatim; its question is open-ended, so the options are written for this vault. Keyed from the module's reveal slides, whose answer is quoted.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ms. Thomas returns 6 months later. Her hot flashes are improved with HRT. However, she now feels a sharp, tearing sensation with intercourse and feels significant vaginal dryness.

stem: Describe your approach to management.

options.html: Stop her systemic MHT, since new pain with intercourse means the estrogen dose is too high
Pain and relationship history, a pelvic exam for atrophy or lichen sclerosus, then LET or a steroid
Double her systemic estrogen dose, since GSM persisting on MHT means her systemic dose is too low
Start ospemifene without an exam, since GSM is a clinical diagnosis that needs no inspection at all

answer:
The correct answer is B. The module's answer: "Take a complete history, focusing on the pain and relationship status · Complete a pelvic examination, assessing for atrophy or other vulvar conditions such as lichen sclerosus · Offer LET for atrophy (can take concurrently with HRT), high-potency steroid for LS."

The reasoning below is mine, from 03 - Clinical Approach to Menopause:

  • ⭐ Systemic MHT can under-treat GSM - it penetrates urogenital tissue poorly - so a woman whose flashes are controlled can still need LET alongside it. That is why A and C are wrong: her MHT is doing its job, and the dryness is treated locally.
  • D: ⭐ examine the vulva if she has GSM symptoms, to r/o skin conditions - a tearing sensation fits atrophy, but also lichen sclerosus, which is treated with a high-potency steroid, not estrogen.
  • The history covers the relationship because post-menopausal sexual problems are often about more than the tissue - health, mood and the partner - and the older note says to interview both where possible.

lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 9-11, leaving out the caption that names the diagnosis, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 45-year-old woman presents with increasing abdominal girth, vague abdominal pain, and fatigue; she feels generally unwell. Examination and imaging show an ovarian mass. The resected specimen is enormous (it arrives in a bucket). Opened, it is a multiloculated cyst filled with thick, jelly-like fluid, and histology shows a single layer of tall columnar cells with mucin-filled cytoplasm resting on the cyst wall, with no invasion of the underlying stroma.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The deck's reveal slide (11) captions the specimen "Benign Mucinous Tumor". Mucin-filled tall columnar cells make it mucinous, and a multilocular, jelly-filled cyst big enough to arrive in a bucket is the mucinous cystadenoma the note describes ("multi-locular cyst filled with mucoid or jelly-like fluid", "often become very large and can extend up into the abdomen"). A serous cystadenoma (A) is a cyst of clear fluid lined by a single layer of bland cuboidal cells. A mucinous carcinoma (B) needs invasive glands in the stroma, and this lining sits on the cyst wall without invading it. A serous borderline tumour (D) is serous, and it shows papillary excrescences with complex architecture and atypical cells (slides 16-18), where this lining is a single bland layer. Naming rule from slide 14: cell subtype + architecture + behaviour = mucinous cyst-adenoma, benign.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 52-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, and imaging shows an ovarian mass, which is surgically resected. The cyst wall is studded with papillary excrescences. On histology there are complex, branching papillae lined by stratified cells with atypical nuclei, sitting on the cyst wall; there is no frank invasion of the stroma.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The deck's reveal slide (17) captions the histology "Serous Borderline Tumor", and slide 18 defines the entity by the three features in this case: complex architecture, atypical cytology, no frank invasion. It is pre-cancerous, treated by surgical excision with a very good prognosis in most, but slide 19 lists its complications: implants (serous subtype only), adhesions, recurrence and progression to low-grade carcinoma. A serous cystadenoma (A) is benign, a single bland layer with no papillary excrescences and no atypia. A low-grade serous carcinoma (C) is where a borderline tumour can end up (slide 19), but a carcinoma needs stromal invasion (slide 20, "Stroma Invasion"); papillae on the cyst wall are not enough. A serous cystadenofibroma (D) is, by the naming rule on slide 14, cystic, fibrous and benign, and has no atypical cells.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 25-year-old presents with abdominal pain for the last 6 months. Pelvic examination finds a unilateral ovarian mass. At surgery the cyst is opened and contains matted hair, greasy sebaceous material and a tooth-like structure; histology shows skin with adnexal structures and cartilage, all of it mature tissue.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Slides 30-31 caption the specimen "Mature Cystic Teratoma", and slide 32 gives the profile: germ cell lineage, young women, common, "dermoid cyst", a mix of mature tissues, benign. Hair, sebum and a tooth in a cyst, with skin and cartilage on histology, are that mix of mature tissues. An immature teratoma (A) is malignant and is defined by primitive (typically neural) tissue, which this specimen lacks. A dysgerminoma (B) is made of undifferentiated germ cells and a yolk sac tumour (C) of extra-embryonic tissue; both are malignant germ cell tumours whose serum markers (LDH +++ and α-FP +++, slide 35) the deck says to send in a young woman with an ovarian mass, but neither forms skin, hair or cartilage.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 57-year-old woman is undergoing hysterectomy for leiomyomas. An incidental ovarian mass is found and sent for intraoperative consultation. The cut surface is uniformly firm, white and well circumscribed; frozen-section histology shows whorled bundles of bland spindle cells with no epithelial component.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The deck's reveal slide (38) captions the specimen "Fibroma", and slide 54 gives its profile: "Firm white nodular mass (common; benign)". Whorled bland spindle cells with no epithelium are the histology, and an incidental find during a hysterectomy for something else is how it usually turns up. A granulosa cell tumour (B) is yellow, solid and cystic with haemorrhage, and its cells form microfollicles (slides 41-42). A serous cystadenofibroma (C) is, by the naming rule on slide 14, an epithelial tumour that is cystic and fibrous; this mass has neither cyst nor epithelium. A Krukenberg tumour (D) is also solid and white, but it is bilateral and made of signet ring adenocarcinoma cells, not spindle cells (slides 50, 55).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 63-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows atypical hyperplasia, and imaging shows an adnexal mass. She undergoes hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. The uterus contains an endometrial carcinoma. The ovarian mass is yellow, solid and cystic with areas of haemorrhage; histologically it is made of small uniform cells arranged in microfollicles that resemble the normal ovarian follicle.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of the ovarian mass?
answer: The correct answer is D. The deck's reveal slide (42) captions the ovarian histology "Granulosa Cell Tumor", beside a drawing of the normal follicle its microfollicles resemble, and slide 43 says it "may produce exogenous estrogen". That estrogen is what ties the ovarian mass to the atypical hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma the deck shows first (slide 40); the note: endometrial cancer "might be the first sign of a GCT". A serous carcinoma (B) is the trap: it is also a tumour of older women, solid and cystic with haemorrhage, but it is invasive epithelium rather than microfollicles, and it makes no estrogen. A fibroma (A) is firm, white and hormonally silent. A mature cystic teratoma (C) is a germ cell tumour of young women, filled with hair and sebum.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 63-year-old woman, whose adnexal mass proved to be a granulosa cell tumour after hysterectomy and BSO for atypical endometrial hyperplasia with an endometrial carcinoma.

stem: Which statement about the behaviour of this ovarian tumour is correct?

options.html: It is benign and does not recur once the involved ovary is removed at surgery
It is malignant with rapid growth, so recurrence is expected within the first year
It is malignant but slow growing, and may recur more than 10 years later
It is benign but produces androgens, so virilization is the usual presenting feature

answer: The correct answer is C. Slide 43 lists four facts: "Malignant, but slow growth", "Late recurrence (>10 yr)", "Prone to rupture (hemoperitoneum)", "May produce exogenous estrogen". A and D call it benign, which it is not; D also names the wrong hormone (the deck says estrogen, and this patient's endometrium proves it). B has the tempo backwards: slow growth with late, not early, recurrence.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 60-year-old woman presents with abdominal discomfort and distension. She has ascites, and imaging shows bilateral nodular ovarian masses. At surgery both ovaries are replaced by a solid and cystic mucinous tumour, and histology shows atypical mucinous glands, dirty and necrotic, infiltrating the ovarian stroma.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Primary mucinous carcinoma of the ovary
Mucinous carcinoma metastatic from the appendix
Krukenberg tumour metastatic from the stomach
High-grade serous carcinoma from the fallopian tube

answer: The correct answer is B. The deck follows this patient from "Mucinous Adenocarcinoma" in both ovaries (slide 47) to "Appendiceal Origin" (slide 48: the appendix distended by the same neoplastic mucinous epithelium) to "Pseudomyxoma Peritonei" (slide 49, the abdomen filled with gelatinous mucin), and slide 55 states the rule: "Beware of the bilateral atypical mucinous tumor (check that appendix!)". A primary mucinous carcinoma (A) is the trap: slide 21 says bilaterality is common in ovarian carcinoma except mucinous, so a bilateral mucinous tumour argues for a metastasis, and slide 52 lists the appendix first among the GI sources. A Krukenberg tumour (C) is also a bilateral metastasis, but its ovaries are solid and white and made of signet ring cells, not glands (slide 50). A high-grade serous carcinoma (D) is the commonest ovarian cancer and often bilateral, but it is serous, not mucinous.

lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to and Pathology of a Pelvic Mass deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slide 50, leaving out the caption that names the diagnosis, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The deck's third part goes on to a second pair of bilateral ovarian masses. Both ovaries are enlarged, solid and uniformly white on the cut surface, and histology shows cells distended by mucin, each with its nucleus pushed to one side, infiltrating the ovarian stroma.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The deck's reveal slide (50) captions these ovaries "Krukenberg tumor", slide 51 shows the ulcerated stomach tumour they came from ("Gastric Origin"), and slide 55 names the pattern: "Krukenberg tumor (signet ring adenocarcinoma)". Mucin pushing the nucleus to the edge of the cell is the signet ring, and involvement of both ovaries is the metastatic pattern (slide 52: "more likely bilateral, multi-nodular"). A fibroma (B) is also firm and white, but it is a benign tumour of bland spindle cells with no mucin. A primary mucinous carcinoma (C) forms glands, and it is the carcinoma that is rarely bilateral (slide 21). A dysgerminoma (D) is a malignant germ cell tumour of young women, made of undifferentiated germ cells, with a raised LDH (slide 35).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 30 year old female with a previous renal transplant on mycophenolate is seen before a planned pregnancy.

stem: Which of the following best describes the fetal risk if she is exposed to mycophenolate during the pregnancy?

options.html: About 40% of exposed pregnancies transmit the exposure to the fetus, and most affected infants are asymptomatic at birth
About 25% of exposed pregnancies result in a malformation, and about 50% end in spontaneous abortion
About 30-50% of exposed pregnancies are affected, but only if the exposure falls in the last 3 months of pregnancy
The risk cannot be quantified because no controlled studies have been conducted in either animals or humans

answer: The correct answer is B. The deck's own case slide gives the two figures: ~25% of exposed pregnancies will result in a malformation and ~50% spontaneous abortion. A (40% vertical transmission, most asymptomatic at birth) is the vault note's figure for a first CMV infection in pregnancy; C (30-50% in the last 3 months) is its figure for genital HSV contracted in the 3rd trimester; D is the wording of FDA category C, and the deck does not say the mycophenolate risk is unquantified - it quantifies it.

lectureMeta: Case from this year's Teratogenesis deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 12-13, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 30 year old female with a previous renal transplant on mycophenolate is seen before a planned pregnancy. About 25% of exposed pregnancies result in a malformation and about 50% in spontaneous abortion.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate pre-conception counselling step for this patient?

options.html: Plan a dose increase now, since drug requirements tend to rise as the pregnancy advances and delivery nears
Stop all of her medications until organogenesis has finished, at the end of the eighth week of gestation
Defer any change until the post-partum visit, when the drug can be switched back to the previous therapy
Consider switching to an alternative medication and minimize the dose and number of therapeutics

answer: The correct answer is D. The deck's pre-conception counselling points are: optimize disease management, optimize other considerations (e.g., 1 mg folic acid daily for antiepileptics), minimize dose and number of therapeutics, consider switching to an alternative medication, and counsel appropriately as to potential teratogenesis. A is the antenatal point (potential dose increases), not pre-conception. B contradicts "optimize disease management" - a transplant patient cannot simply stop immunosuppression, and the deck never advises stopping all drugs. C is the post-partum point (switch back to previous therapeutics); the whole point of the case is that the decision is made before conception.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A woman is currently pregnant. Her obstetric history is a 38 week livebirth and a 32 week stillbirth.

stem: What is this patient's GTPAL?
answer: The correct answer is B. The slide prints GTPAL 31101 and G/P 3/2. G counts every pregnancy including the current one (3). The 38 week birth is term (T1). The 32 week stillbirth was carried past 20 weeks and before 37, so it counts as preterm (P1) and as a delivery for Para, but it is not a living child, so L is 1, not 2. Option A counts the stillbirth as term; option C counts it as living; option D leaves out the current pregnancy.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A woman is currently pregnant. Her obstetric history is a 10 week miscarriage, 36 week liveborn twins, and a 41 week liveborn singleton.

stem: What is this patient's GTPAL?
answer: The correct answer is D. The slide prints GTPAL 41113 and G/P 4/2. Four pregnancies including the current one. The 41 week singleton is term (T1). The twins are ONE pregnancy delivered at 36 weeks, so preterm is 1, not 2 (option A), and gravida is 4, not 5 (option B). The 10 week miscarriage is a loss before 20 weeks (A1; option C drops it). Living children are the two twins plus the singleton (L3). Para counts pregnancies delivered past 20 weeks: the twins and the singleton, so 2.

preamble.html: A woman is currently pregnant. She has had 3 previous deliveries between 39 and 40 weeks, and one neonatal death at 10 days of life due to a congenital anomaly.

stem: What is this patient's GTPAL?
answer: The correct answer is A. The slide prints GTPAL 43002 and G/P 4/3. Four pregnancies including the current one; all three prior deliveries were at 39-40 weeks, so all three are term (T3), including the one whose baby died at 10 days: T counts the pregnancy carried to term, not the child's survival. The neonatal death is subtracted from L only (2 living), not moved to A (option C; abortions are losses before 20 weeks) and not counted as living (option B). Option D leaves out the current pregnancy.

lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to Preterm Labour deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 15-17, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are a medical student working with the Obstetrics team at Victoria Hospital. You are about to see Jennifer, a 25yo G3P2 currently at 29+2 who has presented to Labour and Delivery triage with contractions. On history, you elicit that Jennifer has a history of two previous vaginal births, one at 36 weeks and the second at 32 weeks. She has a history of previous cone biopsy because of high risk pap smears at the age of 20. She smokes 1 PPD and does not use any other substances. She has been on vaginal progesterone in this pregnancy for preterm birth prevention.

stem: Which feature of Jennifer's history is NOT a risk factor for preterm birth?

options.html: Her two previous vaginal births, one at 36 weeks and the other at 32 weeks
Her cone biopsy for high risk pap smears at the age of 20
Her use of vaginal progesterone in this pregnancy for prevention
Her ongoing smoking of one pack of cigarettes per day

answer: The correct answer is C. Vaginal progesterone is the one item on the list that is a preterm birth prevention measure, not a risk factor; the deck mentions it only as what she has been on "for preterm birth prevention" (slide 17). The other three are on the deck's own risk-factor slides: previous spontaneous preterm birth (both earlier births were before 37 weeks, slide 15), cervical surgery with "Cone > LEEP" (slide 15), and smoking/substance use (slide 16). The deck does not say why progesterone prevents preterm birth, and that is not covered in the block notes either.

lecture: Deck Case - Approach to Preterm Labour
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to Preterm Labour deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 19-24, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jennifer, a 25yo G3P2 at 29+2, has presented to Labour and Delivery triage with contractions. She has had two previous vaginal births at 36 and 32 weeks, a cone biopsy at age 20, smokes 1 PPD, and is on vaginal progesterone for preterm birth prevention. No history of contractions prior to today. She started cramping this morning and progressed to regular contractions every 5-10 minutes, lasting 30-40 seconds over the last hour. No bleeding, leaking fluid, or infectious symptoms. On physical exam, you perform Leopold's maneuvers and determine that the fetus is in a cephalic presentation. A cervical exam is done and Jennifer's cervix is found to be 2cm dilated and soft. The fetal heart rate is normal. She continues to have contractions every 5-6 minutes.

stem: The team elects to give Jennifer indomethacin. What is the purpose of tocolysis at this point?

options.html: To delay birth by about 48 hours so that antenatal corticosteroids can be given and transfer arranged
To stop the preterm labour altogether so that she can be discharged home and carry to term
To treat the underlying cause of her contractions, which in most patients presenting this way is a uterine infection
To provide fetal neuroprotection and reduce the risk of cerebral palsy in a birth before 34 weeks

answer: The correct answer is A. Slide 22: tocolysis "may delay spontaneous vaginal birth by 48 hours which is enough time to transfer patient to a tertiary care centre and/or administer antenatal corticosteroids". It is a bridge, not a cure (B is wrong). C is wrong because the underlying etiology is often idiopathic (slide 11); infection and UTI are causes to investigate, but a tocolytic does not treat them. D describes magnesium sulfate (slide 31), not a tocolytic. Slide 21 adds the step before the drug: dehydration is a common cause of TPTL symptoms, so rehydrate first and reserve indomethacin, nifedipine or terbutaline for patients who do not respond.

lecture: Deck Case - Approach to Preterm Labour
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to Preterm Labour deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 24-29, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jennifer, a 25yo G3P2 at 29+2, presented to triage with regular contractions and a 2 cm soft cervix. The team gave indomethacin and betamethasone. Her contractions spaced out in Triage and she was admitted to the Antenatal ward for ongoing monitoring. The next day you are on call again and are called as she has had a large gush of clear fluid. Physical examination confirms that Jennifer has PPROM. No overt signs of labour or chorioamnionitis at this time.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management now?

options.html: Start an IV magnesium sulfate bolus and continuous infusion now for fetal neuroprotection
Start antibiotics for pregnancy prolongation and complete the corticosteroid course
Restart indomethacin to prevent labour from beginning in the next 48 hours
Start IV penicillin now for GBS prophylaxis, since her GBS status is unknown

answer: The correct answer is B. Slide 29 is the deck's own answer: "Antibiotics are started for pregnancy prolongation. Corticosteroid course is completed." Slide 28 gives the reason: antibiotics increase the latency from PPROM to delivery, and pregnancy prolongation improves neonatal outcomes; without intervention, 50% of patients with PPROM under 32 weeks deliver within 48 hours and 75% within 7 days. A and D are the interventions for imminent preterm birth (slides 31-33), and she has no signs of labour. C: she is not contracting, so there is nothing to tocolyse; the banked module case (Q107) makes the same point for a patient with PPROM at 28 weeks who is not contracting.

lecture: Deck Case - Approach to Preterm Labour
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to Preterm Labour deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 30-32, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jennifer, a 25yo G3P2, was admitted at 29+2 with threatened preterm labour, received indomethacin and betamethasone, then ruptured her membranes the next day and was started on antibiotics for pregnancy prolongation. One week later you are on call once again and are called to Antenatal as Jennifer is having regular painful contractions. The team assesses her and she is now 6cm dilated with a normal FHR. The baby is still cephalic. Jennifer is transferred to Labour and Delivery for labour management.

stem: Which intervention is now indicated for fetal neuroprotection, and why?

options.html: A repeat course of betamethasone 12 mg IM, to reduce the risk of intraventricular hemorrhage
Nifedipine, to delay the birth until 34 weeks when the fetal brain is more mature
Bolus IV fluids to the mother, to normalize fetal cerebral blood flow during labour
IV magnesium sulfate as a bolus then continuous infusion, to reduce neonatal cerebral palsy

answer: The correct answer is D. Slide 31: magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is "given IV to the mother as a bolus then continuous infusion" and is "shown to decrease the risk of neonatal cerebral palsy if PTB before 34 weeks"; she is about 30+3. Slide 32 lists the proposed mechanisms (stabilization of cerebral circulation, prevention of excitatory injury, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects) and says the mechanism is not well understood. A: the steroid course was already completed (slide 29), and the deck describes steroids as one course of two doses; it does not describe repeat courses. B: tocolysis buys 48 hours, not four weeks (slide 22), and at 6 cm birth is imminent. C: hydration is for the uterine irritability of threatened preterm labour (slide 21), not neuroprotection.

lecture: Deck Case - Approach to Preterm Labour
lectureMeta: Case from this year's Approach to Preterm Labour deck, swept 2026-09-27. The stem is assembled from slides 30 and 33, because the deck poses no question there. Options and reasoning written for this vault from the block's notes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jennifer, a 25yo G3P2, is now about 30+3 with PPROM, 6 cm dilated, regular painful contractions and a normal FHR; the baby is cephalic and she has been transferred to Labour and Delivery. Because she is preterm, she has not yet had her routine 35-37 week GBS swab, so her GBS status is unknown.

stem: What does the lecture recommend for GBS prophylaxis in this situation?

options.html: IV penicillin, first-line if no allergies, because her status is unknown and the birth is preterm
No prophylaxis, because antibiotics are only indicated when a vaginal swab is GBS positive
Send the vaginal swab now and start IV antibiotics only if it returns positive before the birth occurs
Continue the oral antibiotics of the latency protocol, which already cover Group B strep

answer: The correct answer is A. Slide 33: "If vaginal swab shows GBS positive or maternal status is unknown and preterm, then IV antibiotics are recommend to reduce the risk of GBS sepsis in the neonate. Penicillin is first-line if no allergies." B and C both wait for a positive swab, which the deck's "or maternal status is unknown" rule does not require. D is not in the deck: the latency antibiotics (slide 28) are given to prolong pregnancy, and the deck does not say they substitute for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis; the block notes do not settle that either, so the option is offered as unsupported rather than contradicted.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm smooth, mobile breast lump that is still present when she is re-examined after her next menstrual cycle. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. What is the first imaging test?
answer: The correct answer is A. Imaging splits at age 35: under 35 the tissue is too dense and the risk too low for mammography, so ultrasound comes first (MRI only if under 35 and high risk). Over 35, mammogram first ± ultrasound. A persistent lump after the next cycle is what moves a pre-menopausal woman from watching to investigating.

stem: Which feature of a palpable breast lump is most concerning for malignancy?

options.html: Hard and fixed, with irregular borders
Tender in the week before menses
Multiple lumpy areas in both breasts, no mass

answer: The correct answer is B. The worrisome lump is single, hard, immovable, with irregular borders, and over 2 cm. Mobility, cyclical tenderness and multiple bilateral lumpy areas point to benign tissue (fibroadenoma, fibrocystic change); a lump that resolves after the cycle is followed, not investigated.

stem: A woman who is 3 weeks postpartum and breastfeeding has a red, hot, painful, swollen wedge of her right breast and a temperature of 38.4 °C. There is no fluctuant mass. What is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Stop breastfeeding and bind the breasts

answer: The correct answer is C. Lactational mastitis is treated with antibiotics while she keeps breastfeeding and fully empties the breast. Drainage is for an abscess, and only if antibiotics fail. Stopping or suppressing lactation leaves the breast engorged. The 'rule out malignancy' step belongs to non-lactating mastitis.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has a red, scaling, eroded rash of the left nipple and areola that has not responded to 6 weeks of topical steroid. There is no palpable mass. What does this lesion imply?
answer: The correct answer is D. Paget's disease of the nipple looks like eczema of the nipple-areola, and there is always an underlying carcinoma (DCIS or invasive) that has reached the nipple through the ducts. A palpable mass would mean invasive disease. Inflammatory carcinoma looks like diffuse mastitis of the breast, not an eczematous nipple.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has bilateral lumpy, tender breasts with no discrete mass. The lumpiness and pain are worst before each period and settle afterwards. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. Fibrocystic change is physiological: lumpy tissue that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle, ± pain, with no discrete mass. It is non-proliferative (RR x1). A fibroadenoma is a discrete mobile lump; a papilloma presents with bloody discharge; fat necrosis is an irregular mass, often after trauma.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has a profuse, yellow-green, malodorous discharge and vulvar itch. The vaginal pH is 5.5 and the NAAT is positive for Trichomonas vaginalis. What is the correct treatment?
answer: The correct answer is A. Trichomoniasis is an STI: oral metronidazole only (single dose or a week), and treat partners from the last 6 months or it simply returns. The vaginal gel is not as effective for trichomonas. Fluconazole and boric acid are for candida; clindamycin is the BV alternative.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with a new sexual partner reports a fishy vaginal odour, worse after intercourse, with little itch. There is a thin grey discharge coating the vaginal walls, pH 5.0, and clue cells on wet mount. Which statement about her diagnosis is correct?

options.html: It is an STI and partners must be treated
It is not an STI but raises STI risk
Culture is required to confirm it
It is treated only in pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is B. This is bacterial vaginosis (Amsel: pH over 4.5, clue cells, fishy amine odour, thin homogeneous discharge). BV is the #1 infectious vaginitis and is not an STI, but it potentiates acquiring one, which is half the reason to treat it. Culture is not required; treatment is metronidazole (oral or vaginal), and in pregnancy it must be oral.

stem: A 30-year-old woman finishing a course of amoxicillin has intense vulvar itch and burning, and a thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge adherent to the walls. Vaginal pH is 4.0 and the whiff test is negative. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.html: Treat her sexual partner as well

answer: The correct answer is C. Candidiasis: vulvar pruritus and burning, cottage-cheese discharge, pH under 4.5, whiff test negative; antibiotics are a risk factor. All routes work: a topical or intravaginal azole or one oral fluconazole dose. It is not an STI, so partners are not treated; metronidazole is for BV and trichomonas.

stem: A 31-year-old woman's routine cervical cytology reports ASC-H (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude a high-grade lesion). What is the next step?
answer: The correct answer is D. High-grade squamous results (HSIL, ASC-H, SqCC) go straight to colposcopy. Low-grade results (LSIL, ASC-US) are repeated in 6-12 months, with colposcopy if they persist. Vaccination does not replace screening or workup.

stem: A 22-year-old woman had unprotected intercourse 6 days ago. She has a negative pregnancy test and wants emergency contraception. Which option is still effective?
answer: The correct answer is E. The copper IUD works up to 7 days after unprotected intercourse, is the most effective method, and leaves her with ongoing contraception. This year's lecture gives levonorgestrel and ulipristal up to 5 days, levonorgestrel being most effective within 72 hours. So on day 6 only the copper IUD is left.

stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to inserting an IUD?

options.html: PID treated with antibiotics 3 years ago

answer: The correct answer is A. The absolute list is short: pregnancy, current PID or cervicitis, immediately after a septic abortion, a distorted uterine cavity, unexplained bleeding, malignant trophoblastic disease, pelvic TB (and PR+ breast cancer for the hormonal IUD). Smoking, age, nulliparity, HIV and a past PID are distractors, not contraindications.

stem: A 21-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain, dyspareunia, a temperature of 38.4 °C and cervical motion tenderness. Her β-hCG is negative and she is well enough for outpatient care. Which regimen is recommended?

options.html: Azithromycin 1 g orally plus metronidazole for 7 days
Ceftriaxone IM once plus doxycycline for 14 days

answer: The correct answer is B. This is PID: cervical motion tenderness (the chandelier sign), fever, negative β-hCG. The Canadian outpatient regimen is ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg BID for 14 days, ± metronidazole. Admit if she is pregnant, an adolescent, severely ill, has a tubo-ovarian abscess, or fails oral therapy.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has sudden severe right lower quadrant pain and vomiting that began during a spin class. She is afebrile, her β-hCG is negative, her haemoglobin is normal, and a tender right adnexal mass is palpable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. Sudden pain during vigorous activity, a tender adnexal mass, negative β-hCG and a stable haemoglobin is ovarian torsion, a surgical emergency. An enlarged ovary acts like a weighted pendulum. A ruptured ectopic has a positive β-hCG; a ruptured cyst gives a falling haemoglobin; PID is subacute with fever.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has severe cyclic pelvic pain that starts two days before menses and deep dyspareunia. Her pelvic exam is normal. Which statement is correct?

options.html: A normal exam rules out endometriosis
Diagnosis is by laparoscopy and biopsy

answer: The correct answer is D. The gold standard is laparoscopy with biopsy (any 2 of 3: glands, stroma, hemosiderin). Severity does not correlate with pain, and the exam is often normal, so a normal exam rules nothing out. First line is ovulatory suppression with NSAIDs; hysterectomy ± oophorectomy is definitive, not first line.

stem: A 44-year-old woman who has had three children has heavy, painful periods. On bimanual exam the uterus is diffusely enlarged, soft and tender, with no irregular masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. A tender, enlarged, boggy uterus with menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea in a parous woman in her 40s is adenomyosis: endometrium buried deep in the myometrium. Fibroids give a firm, irregular, enlarged uterus. The diagnosis is histological, often only at hysterectomy, which is also the gold-standard treatment.

stem: A 63-year-old woman, 11 years past menopause and not on HRT, has had two episodes of light spotting. Her speculum exam shows atrophic vaginal mucosa and her Pap test last year was normal. What is the most important next investigation?
answer: The correct answer is A. Atrophy is the most common cause of PMB, but endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in every woman with PMB: speculum exam, TVUS and endometrial biopsy. Atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion, and a negative Pap does not end the workup.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has regular 28-day cycles with heavy flow and clots. She wants a non-hormonal treatment she can take only during her period. What is the best option, and its limitation?
answer: The correct answer is B. Tranexamic acid (with an NSAID) is the non-hormonal, as-needed option for heavy menstrual bleeding. It reduces intensity only, not duration or regularity. The other options are hormonal and are taken continuously.

stem: A patient asks what a 'total' hysterectomy removes, compared with a 'subtotal' one. What is the correct answer?

options.html: Total takes the uterus and ovaries; subtotal keeps the ovaries
Total takes the tubes; subtotal keeps them
Total takes the uterus and cervix; subtotal keeps the cervix
Total is abdominal; subtotal is vaginal
Total includes lymph nodes; subtotal does not

answer: The correct answer is C. A total hysterectomy removes the uterus and cervix; a subtotal removes the uterus and keeps the cervix. The tubes (salpingectomy) or tubes plus ovaries (salpingo-oophorectomy) are separate additions, and the route (vaginal, laparoscopic, abdominal) is a different question.

stem: Which patient having a suction D&C should receive routine antibiotic prophylaxis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The same procedure gets two answers: prophylaxis for therapeutic abortion (termination), but not for a D&C done for pregnancy loss, whether missed, incomplete or inevitable. Infection, hemorrhage and retained products are the complications the review stars.

stem: A 33-year-old woman had three D&Cs in a year for retained products. She now has no periods, with a negative pregnancy test and normal FSH, prolactin and TSH. Which step raised her risk most?
answer: The correct answer is E. This is Asherman syndrome: adhesions in the endometrial cavity causing secondary amenorrhea. The risk comes from curettage, above all repeat and sharp curettage, which is why suction is used and sharp curettage is rarely needed, and why retained products are managed with misoprostol where possible.

stem: A woman with an uncertain last period has two early ultrasounds: at 6 weeks (CRL 4 mm) and at 8 weeks (CRL 16 mm). Which measurement should set her due date?
answer: The correct answer is A. Once an embryo is seen, MSD is no longer used and CRL is the most accurate estimate. With several scans, use the earliest with a CRL over 10 mm (about 7 weeks), which here is the 8-week scan. Once set that way the due date is fixed; later scans report growth, not a new date.

stem: A 38-year-old woman at 12 weeks wants a diagnostic test for trisomy 21 as early as possible. Which test fits, and what is its miscarriage risk?
answer: The correct answer is B. At 12 weeks the diagnostic option is CVS (11-13 weeks), with a miscarriage risk of about 1% and a risk of maternal cell contamination and confined placental mosaicism. Amniocentesis (15-20 weeks) carries about 0.5% but cannot be done yet. NIPT and eFTS are screens, not diagnoses: a positive screen always needs a diagnostic test.

stem: At her first prenatal visit a woman is found to be non-immune to rubella. Which vaccine plan is correct?

options.html: MMR now, in the first trimester
Tdap now at the booking visit; MMR at 28 weeks

answer: The correct answer is C. The only vaccines to avoid in pregnancy are the live attenuated ones (MMR, varicella, BCG), so MMR waits until postpartum. Tdap is given at 27-32 weeks so antibodies cross to the baby, and influenza can be given at any gestational age in flu season.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is O-negative with a negative antibody screen at her first visit and has had no bleeding. When should she routinely receive Rh immunoglobulin during the pregnancy?

options.html: Only if the baby is Rh-positive

answer: The correct answer is D. An unsensitized Rh-negative mother gets RhIG routinely at 28-30 weeks, after bleeding, an invasive procedure or trauma, and again postpartum if the baby is Rh-positive. RhIG is prophylaxis only: it does nothing once an antibody already exists.

stem: A woman at 9 weeks has heavy bleeding and cramping. On speculum exam the cervical os is open with tissue in the canal, and ultrasound shows retained tissue in the uterus without a fetal heartbeat. What is the diagnosis?

options.html: Inevitable abortion with a live embryo

answer: The correct answer is E. An incomplete abortion: bleeding, an open os, products partly passed, no fetal heart. Threatened has a closed os and a live embryo; missed is a closed os with retained non-viable products; complete is a closed os with an empty uterus. Management is to remove tissue at the os, then expectant, medical or surgical.

stem: A hemodynamically stable woman has an unruptured 2.5 cm tubal ectopic with a β-hCG of 1800 and no fetal cardiac activity. Which finding is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate?

options.html: She conceived with a copper IUD in place

answer: The correct answer is A. Absolute contraindications to methotrexate include breastfeeding, liver disease or alcoholism, immunodeficiency, blood dyscrasias, renal dysfunction, PUD, acute pulmonary disease and a viable IUP. A previous ectopic and an IUD are risk factors for ectopic pregnancy, not contraindications, and a low β-hCG favours methotrexate success.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with normal blood pressures in the first trimester has a BP of 146/94 at 30 weeks, confirmed 20 minutes later. Urine protein is negative, and she has no symptoms and normal bloodwork. What is the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The line is 20 weeks. Hypertension after 20 weeks, with normal BPs before it and no proteinuria or adverse conditions, is gestational hypertension. Before 20 weeks it would be pre-existing, and with proteinuria it would be pre-eclampsia. Both chronic and gestational hypertension raise the risk of pre-eclampsia.

stem: A woman at 24 weeks with chronic hypertension needs oral antihypertensive treatment. Which drug is appropriate?
answer: The correct answer is C. Oral options are labetalol, nifedipine XL or methyldopa. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated because they are toxic to the fetal kidneys (oligohydramnios, renal failure), and diuretics shrink intravascular volume in a state built for fluid retention. The review slide lists diuretics and ACEi/ARB under management; the lecture contraindicates them.

stem: A woman at 35 weeks has severe pre-eclampsia with headache and hyperreflexia, and the team decides to deliver. What should be started to prevent eclamptic seizures?
answer: The correct answer is D. Magnesium sulfate is the mainstay of seizure prophylaxis: a 4 g load over 20 minutes, then 1-2 g/h until delivery and for 12-48 h postpartum. It raises the seizure threshold. Eclampsia is pre-eclampsia plus seizures. Nifedipine and hydralazine lower BP but do not prevent seizures.

stem: On continuous monitoring, a labouring woman's tracing shows decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and recover only after it ends. What do they indicate?
answer: The correct answer is E. Late decelerations start after the peak and recover after the contraction ends: reduced uteroplacental flow (placental insufficiency), the worrying pattern. Early decelerations mirror the contraction (head compression); variable ones are sharp Vs with no fixed timing (cord compression).

stem: Ten minutes after a vaginal birth, which sign is the earliest that the placenta has separated?

options.html: The uterus becoming firm and globular
A gush of blood from the vagina
Lengthening of the umbilical cord at the introitus
The uterus rising in the abdomen

answer: The correct answer is A. The signs of separation are a firm, globular uterus, a gush of blood, the uterus rising, and the cord lengthening. The firm, globular uterus is the earliest. The third stage runs 2-30 minutes and is actively managed with a uterotonic, gentle cord traction and fundal massage.

stem: A woman at 32 weeks has a sudden painless episode of bright red vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and non-tender and the fetal heart tracing is normal. Her placental location is not yet known. Which step must come before a digital cervical exam?
answer: The correct answer is B. Painless bleeding is placenta previa until the ultrasound says otherwise. Never examine the cervix of a bleeder until ultrasound has shown the placenta is clear of it, because examining a previa can set off massive hemorrhage. In previa the fetus usually stays stable, but the mother is at high risk of becoming unstable.

stem: At 37 weeks, a woman's membranes rupture with a small amount of bleeding, followed at once by fetal bradycardia. She is hemodynamically stable. An earlier scan showed a velamentous cord insertion. Whose blood is it, and what is the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. A small bleed with fetal distress out of keeping with the volume is fetal blood: vasa previa. Unprotected umbilical vessels cross the cervix (type 1 is a velamentous cord insertion). A small volume is a large share of the fetal blood volume. The Apt test shows fetal blood in the vaginal bleed.

stem: A woman at 34 weeks with pre-eclampsia has sudden severe abdominal pain, dark vaginal bleeding, and a tender, firm uterus contracting frequently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Painful bleeding with a tender, sometimes rigid uterus is abruption: premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall. Hypertension is a risk factor. Blood irritates the myometrium, so labour may follow, and consumptive coagulopathy and hypovolemia are the threats. Previa and vasa previa are usually painless.

stem: Fifteen minutes after a vaginal birth following a 20-hour labour on oxytocin, a woman is bleeding heavily. The fundus is soft and boggy above the umbilicus. What is the most likely cause and first step?

options.html: Retained placental tissue; manual removal and D&C
Uterine atony; fundal massage and uterotonics

answer: The correct answer is E. Tone (uterine atony) is the primary cause of PPH, and prolonged labour and prolonged oxytocin are risk factors for it. A soft, boggy uterus calls for bimanual exam, fundal massage and uterotonics (oxytocin first line), then TXA. A firm uterus would send you looking for trauma. The 4 T's are tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin.

stem: A woman at 29 weeks is 7 cm dilated with regular contractions, and birth is expected within hours. She got betamethasone yesterday. Which drug, given now, reduces the baby's risk of cerebral palsy?
answer: The correct answer is A. When preterm birth is imminent (under 34 weeks), an IV bolus and infusion of magnesium sulfate gives fetal neuroprotection (fewer cases of cerebral palsy), with penicillin if GBS is positive or unknown. Tocolytics only delay birth by about 48 hours to allow steroids and transfer. Betamethasone supports lung maturation.

stem: A woman at 30 weeks reports a gush of fluid. There is pooling on speculum exam, with positive nitrazine and ferning. She is not contracting and has no sign of chorioamnionitis. What is the purpose of the antibiotic course she is given?

options.html: To lengthen the time until delivery
To speed fetal lung maturation before birth

answer: The correct answer is B. This is PPROM (rupture before 37 weeks), diagnosed by pooling, nitrazine and ferning. Antibiotics increase the latency from PPROM to delivery, and that prolongation improves neonatal outcomes. She also gets a course of steroids. Deliver if she labours or develops chorioamnionitis.

stem: On day 3 after an emergency cesarean, a woman has a temperature of 38.6 °C on two readings, uterine tenderness and foul lochia. She is otherwise stable. What is the most common postpartum complication, and the oral treatment for this one?
answer: The correct answer is C. Puerperal infection is the most common postpartum complication: a temperature over 38 °C on any 2 of the first 10 days, excluding the first 24 hours. Endometritis is the usual source and is far more common after a non-elective C/S. Treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate, or clindamycin plus gentamicin IV if septic.

stem: A mother is tearful, irritable and sleeping poorly 4 days after birth, and still bonding well with her baby. Which feature would make postpartum depression, not blues, the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Postpartum blues affect up to 85% of mothers, start in the first days and are self-limited, within about 2 weeks. Blues lasting over 2 weeks, or severe within the first 2, point to postpartum depression. Screen with PHQ-2, then EPDS or PHQ-9.

options.html: Reassure, since SFH normally varies by up to 4 cm

answer: The correct answer is E. From 20 weeks the SFH in cm should match the weeks, and a lag of over 2-3 cm is suspect (here 4 cm, with a maternal risk factor). SFH only suggests: ultrasound EFW is the only confirmation. An EFW under the 10th percentile then leads to umbilical artery Doppler, amniotic fluid volume and an NST.

stem: A mother on day 5 postpartum asks what now drives how much milk she makes. What is the answer?

options.html: Removal of milk from the breast
Oxytocin released with each let-down reflex

answer: The correct answer is A. Lactation needs prolactin, oxytocin and removal of milk. Early lactogenesis is under hormonal control, but from about day 3 control is autocrine: removal drives supply. That is why removal must start early and why poor extraction lowers production. Breast size does not matter.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Meera is a 22 year old G0 who presents for an assessment as a new patient in your practice. She works as an administrative assistant for the municipality. She lives with her boyfriend of 2 years and has been sexually active for 4 years.

stem: Does Meera need cervical screening? What are the current screening guidelines for cervical cancer screening? When does screening end? (Cancer Care Ontario, 2025)

options.html: Yes, since she has been sexually active for 4 years; start cytology now and repeat it every 3 years
Not yet; screening starts at about 25, with a primary HPV test repeated every 5 years if negative
Yes, since screening starts at 21 for anyone sexually active, with an HPV test every 3 years
Not yet; screening starts at 25 with cytology, and HPV is only tested after an abnormal result

answer:
B. Reasoned from 06 - Cervical Cancer Screening.

  • ⭐ She becomes eligible at 25. Sexual debut doesn't change that. Slide 25: "Any asymptomatic person with a cervix who has ever been sexually active is invited to join Canadian cervical cancer screening programs at ≈ age 25 (depending on jurisdiction)." Four years of sexual activity makes her eligible once she turns 25, which is why A and C are wrong.
  • ⭐ The test is HPV first. Slide 47: "Molecular Testing for High Risk HPV · Cytology Triage only if High Risk HPV present." That rules out D, which describes the old cytology-first programme.
  • The interval: the lecture's algorithm (slide 48, Zigras et al., Curr Oncol 2023) sends an HPV-negative result to "Return to screening in 5 yrs." ⭐ The high negative predictive value is what buys the longer interval (slide 44).

⚠ When screening ends is not in the block. The DSSG asks it, and neither the lecture nor any Repro note states a stopping age. It is left open for the facilitator rather than filled in here.

stem: 3 years pass and she is now 25 years old. Her cervical HPV screening test is conducted and found to be HPV negative. If she wasn’t immunosuppressed what is the routine screening interval.

Every year while immunosuppressed, and every 3 years routinely after a negative HPV test

Every 3 years either way, since HPV testing has a lower positive predictive value than cytology

No letter is keyed. The block settles only half of this question. Reasoned from 06 - Cervical Cancer Screening.

  • ⭐ The routine interval is 5 years. The lecture's algorithm (slide 48) returns an HPV-negative result to "screening in 5 yrs". That rules out B and D. D also misuses a true fact: HPV testing's lower PPV is why cytology is kept as the triage step (slide 44), not a reason to screen more often.
  • ⚠ The block has no screening interval for immunosuppression. The lecture gives immunocompromise a 3-dose vaccine schedule (slide 20) but no screening interval, so the notes can't choose between A and C. A is the likelier intended answer, because the DSSG wouldn't mention her immunosuppressant if it changed nothing. Confirm with the facilitator.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
Meera is a 22 year old G0 who presents for an assessment as a new patient in your practice. She works as an administrative assistant for the municipality. She lives with her boyfriend of 2 years and has been sexually active for 4 years.

Meera has heard about the HPV vaccination and recalls that she did not get it through the school program.

stem: Can she get it even though she is already sexually active? If she gets the HPV vaccination, will she continue to need cervical screening?

options.html: No, since the vaccine is only offered before sexual debut; she simply carries on screening
Yes, and once vaccinated she can stop screening, since Gardasil-9 covers the high-risk types
Yes, and a single dose is enough at her age; screening can then be spaced out to 10 years
Yes, and she still needs screening; on an immunosuppressant she gets the 3-dose schedule

answer:
D. Reasoned from 06 - Cervical Cancer Screening.

  • She can have it. The note: "HPV vaccination is available up to age 45. There are still benefits in older individuals, even if they have been exposed to HPV and even if they have pre-cancerous lesions." The school programme aims at grade 7 because younger adolescents are less likely to have been exposed and respond better. It isn't because the vaccine stops working after sexual debut. That rules out A.
  • ⭐ She still needs screening. Slide 21: "Vaccination does not replace cervical screening - even if vaccinated, eligible individuals should still be screened." That rules out B.
  • ⭐ Her immunosuppression sets the dose, not her age. Slide 20: age 21-26 is a 2-dose schedule, but immunocompromised → 3-dose. A single dose (C) is the schedule for ages 9-20, and no interval in the lecture is 10 years.
