preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Meera is a 22 year old G0 who presents for an assessment as a new patient in your practice. She works as an administrative assistant for the municipality. She lives with her boyfriend of 2 years and has been sexually active for 4 years.

stem: Meera returns at the age of 30 for repeat cervical HPV screening. Her HPV test returns as positive (HPV 16) and her reflex cytology reports ASCUS. A) What is the next recommended management step? B) What would be the recommended management if HPV was positive (non 16, 18 or 45) and reflex cytology was ASCUS?

options.html: Repeat the HPV test in 1 year; for another high-risk type with ASCUS, refer to colposcopy
Repeat cytology in 6-12 months; for another high-risk type with ASCUS, screen again in 5 years
Refer to colposcopy; for another high-risk type with ASCUS, repeat the HPV test in 1 year
Refer to colposcopy; for another high-risk type with ASCUS, refer to colposcopy as well

answer:
C. Reasoned from the lecture's algorithm, slide 48 of 06 - Cervical Cancer Screening (Zigras et al., 2023).

  • ⭐ HPV 16 goes to colposcopy whatever the cytology shows. In the algorithm, "HPV 16/18 Positive → Reflex LBC → Refer to colposcopy". The reflex cytology is still done, but no result sends her anywhere else. That rules out A and B.
  • ⭐ Any other high-risk type with ASCUS gets a repeat HPV test in 1 year. "HPV Other Positive → Reflex LBC → Normal/ASCUS/LSIL → Repeat HPV test in 1 yr". Only ASC-H, HSIL, AGC or AIS goes straight to colposcopy. That rules out D.
  • B is the old cytology rule ("repeat in 6-12 months" for a low-grade result), applied after the programme has changed.
  • The algorithm's footnote: "Individuals who are under screened or never screened may be at high risk for immediate CIN3+ and therefore may warrant immediate referral to colposcopy."

⚠ The DSSG and the lecture group the genotypes differently. The DSSG says "non 16, 18 or 45". The lecture's algorithm names HPV 16/18 only, and puts every other type, 45 included, under "HPV Other". It doesn't change this answer, since Meera's is HPV 16, but it would change what happens with an HPV 45 result. Flagged, not reconciled.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jackie is a 32 year old healthy G3 T3 P0 A0 L3 living at home with her husband and 3 children. She works part-time as an ECE. She comes to clinic with complaints of heavy bleeding during her menstrual period.

stem: Describe your approach to taking her history with respect to her bleeding.

options.html: Her family history of gynecologic cancer first, since heavy bleeding at 32 is usually malignant
Only the number of pads she uses a day, since flow volume alone classifies heavy bleeding
Her bowel and bladder symptoms first, since heavy bleeding is usually referred from the gut
Vitals first, then frequency, duration and flow against her old pattern, and pregnancy

answer:
D. Reasoned from 15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain.

  • ⭐ Check she is stable first. "You must first ensure that they are stable. Check vitals first - everything else waits on that."
  • Then characterise the bleeding against her usual pattern. AUB is "any change in frequency, duration, amount of flow, and/or bleeding between cycles". The lecture's teaching case shows why: "previously 28-day cycles with a pad every 4 hours, now 14-45 day cycles with a pad more than hourly, flooding and clots. Nobody had asked." Pad count is one part of that, which is why B falls short.
  • Then a full gynecologic and obstetric history, and keep pregnancy in mind: "do not forget 'Baby' sitting across the whole framework." She is G3 T3, so it is a live question.
  • A gets her age wrong. Malignancy rises in the perimenopause, which is why the biopsy rule starts at 40. C isn't in either note.

⚠ Thin in the block. Neither note has a structured history checklist for heavy bleeding, such as a bleeding chart or a coagulopathy screen.

stem: What medical conditions could affect her bleeding?

options.html: Von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, liver disease, leukemia, hypothyroidism and PCOS
Asthma, migraine, eczema and seasonal allergies, since all of them raise prostaglandin release
None: fibroids and polyps are the causes, since medical conditions do not change menstrual flow
Hypertension and type 2 diabetes, since both of them act directly on the endometrial vessels

answer:
A. Reasoned from 15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain.

  • ⭐ The C and the E of PALM-COEIN. Coagulopathy: "vWD, thrombocytopenia, liver, leukemia". Endocrine: "PCOS, TSH, PRL, Cushing syndrome". The pathology note says the same: "A coagulopathy can cause abnormal uterine bleeding (e.g. heavy periods): von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia, liver disease, leukemia."

  • C is wrong because the question asks about medical conditions, and structural lesions are only the PALM half of the framework. B and D are not on the list.

preamble.html: Jackie is a 32 year old healthy G3 T3 P0 A0 L3 living at home with her husband and 3 children. She works part-time as an ECE. She comes to clinic with complaints of heavy bleeding during her menstrual period.

stem: With normal physical examination, what investigations would you order?

options.html: An endometrial biopsy for everyone, since heavy bleeding at any age needs tissue first
CBC and beta-hCG, ultrasound in selected patients, and TSH or coagulation if indicated
CA-125 and a CT of the pelvis, since heavy bleeding needs malignancy excluded by imaging
No tests at all, since a normal exam means her bleeding is dysfunctional and needs none

answer:
B. Reasoned from 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain and 15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding.

  • With no lesion seen, the pathology flowchart goes to "CBC (Hgb), beta hCG, pap test if indicated · ultrasound in selected patients". The AUB note's longer list adds "CBC, INR, PTT · FSH, LH, estradiol · TSH, PRL", which are the tests for the conditions in the previous question.
  • ⭐ She is 32, so she doesn't automatically get a biopsy. "Every patient over 40 with AUB gets an endometrial biopsy." That is why A is wrong for her.
  • C: "Ultrasound is the main imaging modality in OBGYN, as it can visualize the pelvic structures better than CT, and has no radiation risk."
  • D: DUB is "a diagnosis of exclusion". You only reach it after the tests, so a normal exam doesn't replace them.

⚠ Not in the block. Ferritin doesn't appear anywhere in Weeks 4-5; iron shows up only as a treatment. The notes also give no biopsy criteria for patients under 40.

stem: Describe a management approach for abnormal uterine bleeding

options.html: Hysterectomy first, since she has completed her family and it cures heavy bleeding outright
A GnRH agonist first, since Lupron is immediate and effective with few side effects at 32
Start conservatively with iron, TXA or ibuprofen, then hormones, ablation, surgery last
Tranexamic acid alone and long term, since it corrects intensity, duration and regularity

answer:
C. Reasoned from 15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding.

  • ⭐ "Always start conservatively - medications - and move up the chain to minimally invasive surgery." The lecture's tiers:
TierOptionsWhen
Non-hormonaliron · cyclokapron (TXA) · ibuprofenMild - start here
HormonalOCP · Depo · Mirena · Visanne · GnRH agonistModerate
Minimally invasiveuterine artery embolization · endometrial ablationFailed medical
SurgeryVH · LAVH · TAHLast
  • A skips the whole ladder. Surgery comes last, even though her family is complete.
  • B: Lupron is "immediate and effective, but a high side-effect profile and very costly".
  • D: TXA is "prn only, but costly, and it only reduces the intensity - not the duration and not the regularity".
  • Progestins, including the hormonal IUD, work as a "'lawnmower' for the endometrium". The DSSG's handout doesn't rank the options, and neither does the lecture outside adolescence.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jackie is a 32 year old healthy G3 T3 P0 A0 L3 living at home with her husband and 3 children. She works part-time as an ECE. She comes to clinic with complaints of heavy bleeding during her menstrual period.

stem: If you visualized a bleeding area on the cervix, how would you approach differ?

options.html: Carry on with cervical screening on schedule, since a routine HPV test will pick the lesion up
Order an endometrial biopsy, since cervical bleeding is almost always endometrial in origin
Nothing changes, since a bleeding point on the cervix does not alter the AUB differential
A structural cause now: examine the lesion, test for cervicitis, and biopsy or remove it

answer:
D. Reasoned from 13 - Approach to Pathology of AUB & Pelvic Pain, 15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding and 06 - Cervical Cancer Screening.

  • ⭐ A visible lesion changes which branch of the flowchart you're on. "A mass at the cervical os narrows the differential to the structural causes (Anatomic, Baby, Neoplasia) and away from the functional ones." The step after that: "Remove the lesion / Send the ENTIRE specimen to pathology." That is why C is wrong.
  • What it could be: infection ("cervicitis", "chlamydia"), or neoplasia ("CIN / carcinoma"). A biopsy can be done by "colposcopy".
  • ⭐ A is the trap. "Cervical screening is NOT for symptomatic people - only asymptomatic patients should be screened." A bleeding cervix is a symptom, so it gets investigated now.
  • B points at the wrong organ once the source has been seen.

⚠ Thin in the block. The notes don't say outright to send a visible cervical lesion straight to colposcopy. Colposcopy is tied to abnormal screening results and listed as a way to biopsy.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Melissa is a 23 year old G0 working at Tim Hortons. She attends your clinic with a complaint of significant increase in pelvic pain that she states has been present for a few years.

stem: What components on history do you need to elicit with respect to her pain?

options.html: Onset, site, character, radiation, timing against her cycle, dyspareunia, GI and GU symptoms
Only her pain score today, since her chronic pain has already been worked up by other doctors
Her family history alone, since chronic pelvic pain is mostly inherited endometriosis
Only whether it is cyclic, since a non-cyclic pain rules out every gynecologic cause

answer:
A. Reasoned from 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain and 11 - Clinical Approach to Acute Pelvic Pain.

  • This is chronic pelvic pain: "pelvic pain (i.e., below the umbilicus) for at least 6 months, that is severe enough to cause functional disability or require treatment."
  • The pain history is the same as for acute pain: "onset / duration / quality / location / radiation / aggravating or alleviating factors / associated symptoms (e.g., GI, GU, fever, discharge, bleeding, etc.)", then the medical, surgical, gynecologic and social history.
  • ⭐ The timing against her cycle points toward a cause. Primary dysmenorrhea hurts "with (not before) menses". In endometriosis the pain "usually begins before (~2 days before) menses", and "dyspareunia is common". Myofascial pain is "NOT related to the cycle at all".
  • D: non-cyclic pain sends you to the review of systems for "GI or nephrologic symptoms". It doesn't rule out gynecologic causes. Myofascial pain and adhesions are both on the list.
  • B is the opposite of the lecture's advice: "these patients might have seen numerous specialists... it is important to listen to their stories."

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Melissa is a 23 year old G0 working at Tim Hortons. She attends your clinic with a complaint of significant increase in pelvic pain that she states has been present for a few years.

stem: How can you determine how it is affecting her life?

options.html: Rely on her pain score alone, since its intensity tells you how much tissue damage there is
Ask what it stops her doing, since CPP is defined by disability or needing treatment
Stage her endometriosis at laparoscopy, since the severity of disease tracks her pain
Count the shifts she has missed at work, since only lost employment counts as disability

answer:
B. Reasoned from 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain and 10 - Endometriosis.

  • ⭐ Function is part of the definition: "severe enough to cause functional disability or require treatment". The treatment goal is "pain reduction and improved function", so function is what you measure.
  • A: "the pain intensity is often not proportional to the actual tissue damage present."
  • C: "The severity of disease does not necessarily correlate with the degree of pain."
  • D is too narrow a measure. Mood and sleep matter too: the differential lists "major depressive disorder" and "sleep disorders", and "many of them feel frustrated and hopeless."

⚠ Not in the block. The notes name no functional questionnaire or scale.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Melissa is a 23 year old G0 working at Tim Hortons. She attends your clinic with a complaint of significant increase in pelvic pain that she states has been present for a few years.

stem: Why is her sexual history important in this case?

options.html: Only sexually active patients get endometriosis, since the disease needs a partner to present
A sexual history replaces the pelvic exam in a patient under 25 with pelvic pain
STIs lead to PID and chronic PID, dyspareunia locates the pain, and abuse is common in CPP
It only changes her contraception, which is the one decision sexual history affects here

answer:
C. Reasoned from 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain, 08 - Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections, 10 - Endometriosis and 16 - Approach to Sexual Health.

  • Infection: "chronic pelvic inflammatory disease" is on the chronic pelvic pain differential, and PID is "initiated by a sexually transmitted agent, and thus is most often seen in sexually active women". "30% of women with chlamydia will develop PID if left untreated." She is under 25, which is an STI risk factor on its own.
  • ⭐ Dyspareunia tells you where the pain is coming from. Superficial pain points to "vulvodynia, atrophy, vulvar skin conditions, vaginismus". Deep pain points to "endometriosis, masses, adhesions, MSK causes". "Many women will not bring up painful intercourse... unless prompted."
  • ⭐ Trauma: "up to 50% of women who suffer from CPP have experienced some kind of abuse/trauma. Therefore, a thorough history is important!"
  • How to take it: the 5 P's ("Partners, Practices, Protection/Past STI, Pregnancy plans, ± Pleasure"), after asking permission.
  • A, B and D are not in the notes, and B contradicts them: the history and the exam go together.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Melissa is a 23 year old G0 working at Tim Hortons. She attends your clinic with a complaint of significant increase in pelvic pain that she states has been present for a few years.

stem: What may you find on physical examination of the pelvis that will help determine theetiology of her problem?

options.html: A normal exam, which rules endometriosis out and points to a bowel cause of her pain instead
A tender, enlarged, boggy uterus, which confirms endometriosis without further workup
Cervical motion tenderness, which confirms endometriosis rather than an infection
Uterosacral nodularity or a fixed uterus, a boggy uterus, or cervical motion tenderness

answer:
D. Each finding points to a different cause. Reasoned from 10 - Endometriosis, 12 - Clinical Approach to Chronic Pelvic Pain and 08 - Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections.

FindingPoints to
⭐ Nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments / cul de sac - "the most specific"endometriosis
Fixed, immobile uterus · an adnexal mass (endometrioma)endometriosis
Tender, enlarged, boggy uterusadenomyosis
Enlarged, firm, irregular, mobile uterusfibroids
Globally tender pelvis, normal uterus, no massesmyofascial pain

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Melissa is a 23 year old G0 working at Tim Hortons. She attends your clinic with a complaint of significant increase in pelvic pain that she states has been present for a few years.

stem: How would you treat Melissa if you suspected PID?

options.html: Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days, ± metronidazole
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 7 days on its own, since chlamydia is the only organism in PID
Laparoscopy first, since PID is best treated surgically to preserve her future fertility
Azithromycin 1 g PO once on its own, since a single dose covers the organisms of PID

answer:
A. Reasoned from 08 - Approach to Sexually Transmitted Infections.

  • ⭐ Outpatient regimen A: "ceftriaxone 250mg intramuscular injection x1 dose PLUS doxycycline 100mg p.o. b.i.d. x 14 days", and "can consider adding metronidazole 500mg p.o. b.i.d. x 14 days". The alternative in the same regimen is cefoxitin 2 g IM with probenecid 1 g PO, plus the same doxycycline.
  • ⭐ Why broad cover: "fewer than 50% of women with PID culture positive for either" chlamydia or gonorrhea. That rules out B and D.
  • C: surgery is "reserved for cases that fail medical treatment or those with tubo-ovarian abscesses", and "PID is NOT easily treated surgically while maintaining fertility."
  • Admit if: other surgical emergencies can't be ruled out, oral therapy fails, severe illness, a tubo-ovarian abscess, immunodeficiency, pregnancy, or a youth or adolescent patient. At 23, check whether she counts as a youth with the facilitator.
  • Also: a beta-hCG before treating, contact tracing, and no sex until both partners are treated. The note states that for chlamydia and gonorrhea, not for PID.

⚠ The condition note disagrees with the lecture. pelvic inflammatory disease gives cefoxitin as "2mg"; the lecture gives 2 g. The lecture's dose is the one used here.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Krista is a 40 year old woman working as an accountant who attends clinic for a “check-up”. She has a long history of abnormal uterine bleeding, but it has not concerned her because her cycles “have always been quite irregular” from when she was a teenager. Since they were so spaced out, she didn’t worry about them too much. She doesn’t really have any major health concerns, but recognizes she needs to lose about 80 pounds to be at a healthier weight. When you ask about a pelvic exam, she declines, because she has never been sexually active.

stem: Krista’s first question is about her chances of pregnancy. How would you counsela 40 year old about this?

options.html: Her fertility is unchanged until menopause, so she can wait and try whenever she is ready
Possible, but fertility falls from about 30 and the miscarriage rate is about 60% over 40
Pregnancy is impossible at 40, so she should go straight to IVF, which restores egg quality
An AMH level will tell her how likely a natural pregnancy is, so check it before counselling

answer:
B. Reasoned from 02 - Fertilization & Infertility and 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS).

  • ⭐ "Fertility starts to decline around age 30 and the decline accelerates from there." "Miscarriage rates rise in step, mostly because of higher rates of aneuploid embryos": 10-15% under 35, about 25% at 35-39, about 60% over 40.
  • C: "in-vitro fertilization does not rescue this, because it is dependent on oocyte age." The notes also say pregnancy with PCOS "may be more difficult... this is certainly possible".
  • D: "AMH measures egg reserve; it does NOT predict natural fertility."
  • ⭐ Her irregular cycles make it urgent. A known cause such as "irregular cycles from PCOS" means referral "immediately - they are unlikely to conceive without ovulation." And "even a 5-10% weight loss can be enough to restart spontaneous ovulation."

⚠ Not in the block. The notes give no pregnancy or live-birth rate per cycle at 40.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Krista is a 40 year old woman working as an accountant who attends clinic for a “check-up”. She has a long history of abnormal uterine bleeding, but it has not concerned her because her cycles “have always been quite irregular” from when she was a teenager. Since they were so spaced out, she didn’t worry about them too much. She doesn’t really have any major health concerns, but recognizes she needs to lose about 80 pounds to be at a healthier weight. When you ask about a pelvic exam, she declines, because she has never been sexually active.

stem: What features on history may direct you as to the cause of her abnormal cycles?

options.html: Her sexual history alone, since having never been sexually active explains irregular cycles
Hot flashes and night sweats alone, since irregular cycles at 40 are always perimenopause
Hirsutism, acne, weight change, galactorrhoea, thyroid symptoms, cycles since menarche
Her diet alone, since cycles irregular from her teens are caused by her current weight

answer:
C. Reasoned from 02 - Fertilization & Infertility, 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) and In-Class - Amenorrhea.

  • The infertility history: "duration, regularity or irregularity of menstrual cycles · weight changes · nipple discharge (e.g., galactorrhea) · acne, hirsutism, oily skin, hair loss pattern (can indicate PCOS) · clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism."
  • ⭐ Cycles irregular since she was a teenager point to PCOS. The PMOS history asks about "age at menarche and how often periods came initially, in the later teens, and after age 20", and "galactorrhoea, whose absence is what removes the prolactinoma". The PCOS clues are "hirsutism, acne, obesity; cycles irregular rather than absent".
  • D: her cycles were irregular long before she gained the weight, and "not all patients with PMOS will be overweight". B fits her age but not a pattern that started in her teens. A has nothing to do with ovulation.

PCOS is taught as PMOS in this year's endocrinology lecture.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Krista is a 40 year old woman working as an accountant who attends clinic for a “check-up”. She has a long history of abnormal uterine bleeding, but it has not concerned her because her cycles “have always been quite irregular” from when she was a teenager. Since they were so spaced out, she didn’t worry about them too much. She doesn’t really have any major health concerns, but recognizes she needs to lose about 80 pounds to be at a healthier weight. When you ask about a pelvic exam, she declines, because she has never been sexually active.

stem: How are you going to evaluate her pelvis?

options.html: Respect her refusal and image the pelvis instead, with a transabdominal ultrasound
Examine her anyway, since a bimanual exam is required before any imaging is ordered
Skip any pelvic assessment, since a patient never sexually active has no pelvic disease
Order a CT of the pelvis, since it shows the endometrium better than an ultrasound

answer:
A. Reasoned from 02 - Fertilization & Infertility and the endocrinology anatomy lecture.

  • "A pelvic ultrasound (e.g., transvaginal ultrasound or transabdominal ultrasound) can be used to give a general overview of the anatomy of the genital tract." The transabdominal route is "the most common method of visualizing the female reproductive tract... and is non-invasive", and "the bladder needs to be quite full".
  • B overrides her refusal.
  • C: she still needs assessment. She has had years of abnormal bleeding and turns 40, and "every patient over 40 with AUB gets an endometrial biopsy" (15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding).
  • D: "Ultrasound is the main imaging modality in OBGYN, as it can visualize the pelvic structures better than CT, and has no radiation risk."

⚠ Thin in the block. No note directly covers a patient who declines the exam or has never been sexually active. It also doesn't say how her weight limits a transabdominal view, or how to get the biopsy without a speculum exam. Worth raising with the facilitator.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Krista is a 40 year old woman working as an accountant who attends clinic for a “check-up”. She has a long history of abnormal uterine bleeding, but it has not concerned her because her cycles “have always been quite irregular” from when she was a teenager. Since they were so spaced out, she didn’t worry about them too much. She doesn’t really have any major health concerns, but recognizes she needs to lose about 80 pounds to be at a healthier weight. When you ask about a pelvic exam, she declines, because she has never been sexually active.

stem: What feature on ultrasound can evaluate her risk of endometrial hyperplasia? Explain.

options.html: Ovarian volume, since enlarged ovaries show how much estrogen she is producing each cycle
Endometrial thickness, since unopposed estrogen from anovulation thickens it
The follicle count, since a count above the cutoff confirms her risk of hyperplasia
Uterine artery flow, since reduced flow shows that the endometrium is not being shed

answer:
B. Reasoned from 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), In-Class - Amenorrhea and 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • ⭐ How it happens: "without ovulation, progesterone is not produced... unopposed estrogen effects on the endometrium → unstable, thickened endometrium → irregular menses." The PMOS lecture puts it as "unopposed estrogen on a chronically anovulatory endometrium is the carcinoma mechanism", and asks for "surveillance for endometrial hypertrophy with ultrasound imaging".
  • Preventing it: "induce withdrawal bleeds at least 4× a year", or "COC or cyclic progestin - oppose the estrogen, protect the endometrium."
  • C is a PCOS finding (follicles on ultrasound), not a measure of the endometrium. A and D measure nothing the notes connect to hyperplasia.

⚠ The 5 mm cutoff does not apply to her. The block's "< 5 mm" normal thickness is for postmenopausal patients not on HRT. The notes give no premenopausal cutoff.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Krista is a 40 year old woman working as an accountant who attends clinic for a “check-up”. She has a long history of abnormal uterine bleeding, but it has not concerned her because her cycles “have always been quite irregular” from when she was a teenager. Since they were so spaced out, she didn’t worry about them too much. She doesn’t really have any major health concerns, but recognizes she needs to lose about 80 pounds to be at a healthier weight. When you ask about a pelvic exam, she declines, because she has never been sexually active.

stem: What risk factors does Krista have for endometrial hyperplasia?

options.html: Never having been sexually active, since HPV exposure is what drives endometrial hyperplasia
Her age alone, since hyperplasia is caused by the decline in estrogen approaching menopause
Obesity, chronic anovulation from likely PCOS, and nulliparity: all unopposed estrogen
Smoking and alcohol, since both raise her circulating estrogen and so thicken the endometrium

answer:
C. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • ⭐ "The risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia are the same as for type 1 endometrial adenocarcinoma, and mostly relate to prolonged unopposed estrogen." The endogenous list: "Obesity · Ovarian origin: PCOS, estrogen-secreting neoplasm (granulosa cell tumor) · Associations: infertility, nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause." Krista has three of them.
  • A: HPV causes cervical disease, not endometrial disease.
  • B reverses the mechanism. It is estrogen without progesterone, not a lack of estrogen.
  • D: neither smoking nor alcohol is on the list.

⚠ Age on its own is not listed. The notes don't list age as a risk factor for hyperplasia. What her age changes is the workup: perimenopause has "higher rates of anovulation and of malignancy", and at 40 her abnormal bleeding qualifies her for an endometrial biopsy (15 - Abnormal Uterine Bleeding).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Grace is a 60 year old woman who lives on her own since her husband died after a heart attack 3 years ago. She sees her 2 children who live in town regularly. She presents with some recent vaginal bleeding. She is healthy, but smokes. Her menopause was at the age of 52 and she has never taken hormone replacement therapy.

stem: What systems can “vaginal” bleeding come from?

options.html: The endometrium only, since after menopause all bleeding is uterine until shown otherwise
The ovaries and tubes, since an adnexal mass is the usual source after menopause
The cervix only, so a normal Pap test settles where her bleeding is coming from
The vulva, vagina, cervix and endometrium, or a fistulising GU or GI malignancy

answer:
D. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • The note's list: "coagulopathy, hormones (HRT), infectious (vaginitis), and neoplasia (vulvar / vaginal / cervical / endometrial; also a fistulising GU or GI malignancy, or radiation damage after a pelvic malignancy)". With atrophy, "the bleeding may be coming from exposed small blood vessels at any of these sites".
  • ⭐ The most common cause is atrophy; the most serious is carcinoma or hyperplasia. "Endometrial carcinoma must be excluded in a woman with PMB." That makes the endometrium the organ to exclude, but not the only source, which is why A is wrong.
  • C: the note answers directly that a negative Pap still needs further investigation.
  • B isn't on the list.

⚠ Not in the block. The notes don't cover urinary or rectal bleeding that is taken for vaginal bleeding, which is what the DSSG's quotation marks suggest. The nearest they come is the fistulising GU or GI malignancy.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Grace is a 60 year old woman who lives on her own since her husband died after a heart attack 3 years ago. She sees her 2 children who live in town regularly. She presents with some recent vaginal bleeding. She is healthy, but smokes. Her menopause was at the age of 52 and she has never taken hormone replacement therapy.

stem: Describe pertinent positive and negative findings from your physical exam of apostmenopausal patient with bleeding.

options.html: Her stability, signs of atrophy, a lesion or mass on speculum exam, and uterine size
A breast and thyroid exam only, since the pelvic exam adds nothing once a TVUS is booked
A bimanual exam only, since atrophy makes a speculum exam too painful to be worthwhile
Hirsutism and galactorrhoea, since bleeding after menopause usually has a hormonal cause

answer:
A. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • Stability first: "is the patient stable?" Then a "general, including abdominal and pelvic exam".
  • ⭐ Always do the speculum exam in the office. It "may reveal an endometrial mass poking through the cervical os, or another cause for the bleeding such as an ulcerated cervical mass". That rules out B and C.
  • Signs of atrophy, the most common cause: "loss of labial fullness · pallor of the urethral and vaginal epithelium · narrow introitus · minimal vaginal moisture · loss of urethral meatal turgor".
  • Uterus: in endometrial cancer "pelvic exam may be normal or may reveal an enlarged uterus", so a normal bimanual is a reassuring negative that doesn't settle anything. The AUB exam adds "bruising and petechiae" and "fixation".
  • D is the premenopausal endocrine exam.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Grace is a 60 year old woman who lives on her own since her husband died after a heart attack 3 years ago. She sees her 2 children who live in town regularly. She presents with some recent vaginal bleeding. She is healthy, but smokes. Her menopause was at the age of 52 and she has never taken hormone replacement therapy.

stem: What investigations would you perform?

options.html: A Pap test, with further workup only if the Pap itself comes back abnormal
A transvaginal ultrasound and an endometrial biopsy, with a speculum exam
A CA-125 and a CT of the abdomen and pelvis to stage her before anything else
FSH, estradiol and TSH, to confirm she is menopausal before any imaging

answer:
B. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • ⭐ The note's summary: "TVUS and endometrial biopsy (and don't forget the speculum exam)." A biopsy is required for "post-menopausal bleeding", a thickness over 5 mm, or recurrent bleeding with a thin endometrium ("4% cancer miss rate" if skipped).
  • Reading the ultrasound: "endometrial cutoff of < 5 mm is the standard for a 'normal' endometrial thickness if the patient is not on HRT". Grace has never taken HRT.
  • Limits of the biopsy: "99.6% sensitivity... but poor detection of polyps and focal lesions because it is done blind."
  • A: a negative Pap still needs further investigation. C stages a cancer that hasn't been diagnosed. D: she has been menopausal for eight years, and that is a clinical diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Grace is a 60 year old woman who lives on her own since her husband died after a heart attack 3 years ago. She sees her 2 children who live in town regularly. She presents with some recent vaginal bleeding. She is healthy, but smokes. Her menopause was at the age of 52 and she has never taken hormone replacement therapy.

stem: If your endometrial biopsy returned as “insufficient sample”, how would you proceed?

options.html: Treat it as a benign result and reassure her, as long as the bleeding stops
Start vaginal estrogen for atrophy, and re-biopsy only if she bleeds again
Repeat the sampling, by office biopsy again or by hysteroscopy or D&C
Refer her straight for hysterectomy, since an empty biopsy suggests cancer

answer:
C. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • ⭐ "Not a benign result - the endometrium has not been sampled; repeat the biopsy (yourself or via a gynecologist, e.g., hysteroscopy or D&C)." That rules out A and B, both of which treat no tissue as if it were a benign result.
  • Hysteroscopy is "useful when a biopsy is not possible in the office". D&C is used when office sampling or hysteroscopy isn't available, but "in 50% of cases, < 60% of the endometrium is sampled".
  • D operates before there is a diagnosis. The next step is getting tissue.

⚠ Not in the block. The notes don't say whether the endometrial thickness changes this step.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Grace is a 60 year old woman who lives on her own since her husband died after a heart attack 3 years ago. She sees her 2 children who live in town regularly. She presents with some recent vaginal bleeding. She is healthy, but smokes. Her menopause was at the age of 52 and she has never taken hormone replacement therapy.

stem: If the sample returned as “atypical endometrial hyperplasia”, how would youcounsel Grace?

options.html: It is benign, so cyclic progestin and a repeat biopsy in a year are all she needs
It is already a cancer, so she needs chemotherapy before any surgery is planned
It comes from atrophy, so vaginal estrogen will reverse it within a few months
Premalignant, often with a concurrent cancer, so a hysterectomy with BSO

answer:
D. Reasoned from 05 - Post-menopausal Woman Presenting with Bleeding.

  • ⭐ "High risk of concurrent or subsequent cancer; referral to a gynecologist; she may need a hysterectomy." The number: "30-40% of patients with complex atypical hyperplasia on biopsy have concurrent adenocarcinoma identified when the hysterectomy is performed." The malignancy risk is "8%" for simple atypical and "29%" for complex atypical hyperplasia.
  • Management: "hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy", "abdominally, laparoscopically or vaginally", with "high-dose progesterone only if surgery is contraindicated". In short, "without atypia, management is medical; with atypia, management is surgical."
  • A is the management for hyperplasia without atypia. B calls it cancer when it is premalignant. C treats the wrong condition, and estrogen is what causes hyperplasia.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Darlene is an 18 year old woman who is completing a victory lap at one of the local high schools. She attends clinic with her mother, who is concerned because she is not menstruating. With her mother present, it is difficult to get a history from Darlene.

stem: Describe how you would confidentially asses Darlene.

options.html: Assure her of confidentiality early, and build rapport and consent before sensitive topics
Take the history from her mother, since the parent's account is the more reliable one
Leave the sexual history for a later visit, since sensitive topics can wait until she is ready
Hand her a validated sexual health questionnaire to fill in while her mother waits with her

answer:
A. Reasoned from 16 - Approach to Sexual Health.

  • ⭐ "Very early on in the discussion, patients should be assured of complete confidentiality." Then "establishing rapport and consent before addressing sensitive topics", and "respecting the patients right to decline answering questions".
  • D: "There is NO standard, validated comprehensive sexual health assessment tool."
  • B is exactly the problem the case sets up. C puts off the one question the workup can't wait for, which is whether she could be pregnant.

⚠ Not in the block. The notes don't say to see an adolescent without the parent present. They also don't cover HEADSS or the limits of confidentiality at 18, though the stem clearly expects both. Leave it for the facilitator.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Darlene is an 18 year old woman who is completing a victory lap at one of the local high schools. She attends clinic with her mother, who is concerned because she is not menstruating. With her mother present, it is difficult to get a history from Darlene.

stem: What is the difference between primary and secondary amenorrhea?

options.html: Primary: no menses by 16 whatever her development; secondary: any missed period after menarche
Primary: none by 13 without, or 15 with, sex characteristics; secondary: 3 months off regular cycles
Primary: no menses by 15 without, or 18 with, sex characteristics; secondary: 12 months without one
Primary: no menses by 13 with, or 15 without, sex characteristics; secondary: 6 months off regular cycles

answer:
B. Reasoned from In-Class - Amenorrhea.

  • ⭐ Primary is "NO prior menses": "no secondary sex characteristics, no menses by age 13", or "with secondary sex characteristics, no menses by age 15 (or within 3 years of thelarche)".
  • ⭐ Secondary is "no period for ≥ 3 months in patients who had previous regular cycles, or ≥ 6 months with at least one spontaneous menstruation, or ≤ 9 periods per year".
  • D swaps the 13 and the 15. The earlier cutoff belongs to the girl without development, because nothing has started at all.
  • A: the vault notes that the Pre-Clerkship Workbook uses "no periods by 16", but the lecture uses 13 and 15.
  • C makes up both numbers.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Darlene is an 18 year old woman who is completing a victory lap at one of the local high schools. She attends clinic with her mother, who is concerned because she is not menstruating. With her mother present, it is difficult to get a history from Darlene.

stem: What physical characteristics might you find in someone presenting with a genetic cause of amenorrhea?

options.html: Low body weight and a heavy exercise load, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
Hirsutism, acne and obesity, as in polycystic ovary syndrome
Short stature, a webbed neck and a shield chest, as in Turner syndrome
Galactorrhoea and bitemporal field loss, as in a prolactinoma

answer:
C. Reasoned from In-Class - Amenorrhea and 05 - Disorders of Growth.

  • ⭐ Turner syndrome is the commonest primary cause (27%), and its clues are "short stature, webbed neck, shield chest". Short stature is "the commonest feature" (95-100%), along with "cubitus valgus, short 4th metacarpals".
  • The other two genetic causes are told apart by the uterus and the pubic hair. "MRKH (46,XX, female range, hair present)" has complete absence of the uterus and cervix. "AIS (46,XY, male range, hair absent)" has breast development but no pubic hair.
  • A, B and D are all real clues from the same table, but for hypothalamic, PCOS and pituitary causes, none of which is genetic.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Darlene is an 18 year old woman who is completing a victory lap at one of the local high schools. She attends clinic with her mother, who is concerned because she is not menstruating. With her mother present, it is difficult to get a history from Darlene.

stem: What laboratory investigations would you perform on Darlene if she presented withsecondary amenorrhea?

options.html: A karyotype first, then an MRI of the pituitary before any hormone levels
FSH and LH alone, since a normal result excludes every other endocrine cause
Estradiol and progesterone alone, repeated on day 21 of two cycles in a row
Beta-hCG first, then FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH and free T4, and androgens

answer:
D. Reasoned from In-Class - Amenorrhea.

  • ⭐ The note's order: "beta hCG before anything else · serum FSH / serum LH · serum prolactin · serum TSH and free T4 · androgens · pelvic ultrasound · karyotype when FSH is high · MRI is not first line". The androgens are "Testosterone, DHEA-S, 17-OHP".
  • A gets the order backwards. A karyotype comes "when FSH is high", and "MRI is not first line".
  • B: FSH sorts the causes rather than excluding them. A high FSH means an ovarian cause, a low FSH means a central one, and "a normal FSH with normal prolactin and TSH points at anovulation, which is where PCOS lives". You need prolactin and TSH to reach that conclusion.
  • C isn't in the workup.

stem: What is the most common cause of amenorrhea in an 18 year old?

options.html: Pregnancy, which has to be excluded before anything else
Turner syndrome, the commonest primary cause at 27%
Polycystic ovary syndrome, the commonest secondary cause at 28%
Imperforate hymen, the commonest outflow tract abnormality

answer:
No letter is keyed. The block doesn't settle which answer the DSSG wants. Reasoned from In-Class - Amenorrhea.

  • ⭐ Pregnancy comes first in the workup: "1st thing to rule out is PREGNANCY !!", "before any other test and whatever the story sounds like". The note never calls it the most common cause, though. It treats pregnancy as a step to clear before the causes are ranked.
  • The ranked causes: "PCOS is the commonest secondary cause (28%), Turner the commonest primary (27%)". "Imperforate hymen" is "the most common outflow tract abnormality".
  • ⚠ The stem doesn't say whether Darlene has ever menstruated, so the notes can't tell primary from secondary for her. A is the likelier intended answer, since she is 18, and the previous question asked about her "if she presented with secondary amenorrhea". Confirm with the facilitator.
